(PDXs) and in vitro organoid models have been used in neuroblastoma. 8–10
However, these methods are time-consuming, and expensive to develop and
maintain.9,11 Moreover, the clinical application of these models is further impeded
by low establishment rates and long establishment times, which often exceed the
median time to progression of four months, as we reported previously.12 Ex vivo
short-term drug screening (in short: short-term screens), where freshly obtained
tumor tissue is briefly cultured before drug screening, offers a rapid alternative,
delivering drug response profiles within a clinically relevant timeframe of 7-24
days after sample collection. 13–15
In this study, we evaluated integrated drug sensitivity and molecular profiling
in different neuroblastoma models to assess their consistency in drug sensitivity
and their potential to guide personalized treatment selection. We performed
short-term and organoid screens and combined this with our previous work on
patient-derived organoids,9 ex vivo short-term screens derived from patients14 or
PDX models. 15 In parallel, in vivo compound testing on matched PDX models was
performed within the ITCC-P4 initiative, a European public-private partnership
evaluating preclinical drug efficacy in pediatric cancer PDX models. 16,17
Furthermore, we included pediatric non-malignant samples to assess non-
selective drug toxicity. Our results demonstrate consistent drug sensitivities
across different neuroblastoma models, assay durations and tissue sources, and
highlight the translational potential of ex vivo short-term drug screening.
Results
Establishment and characterization of short-term, organoid, and
PDX neuroblastoma models
To compare drug sensitivities of pre-clinical neuroblastoma models, 55 drug
screens, from samples originating from 38 patients, were performed at the
Princess Máxima Center (Máxima) or Hopp Children’s Cancer Center (KiTZ)
(Fig. 1A). Four types of drug screens were performed on tumor cells: patient-
derived short-term (n = 8) and organoid (n = 13) screens, and PDX-derived short-
term (n = 17) and organoid (n = 8) screens (Fig. 1B; Supplementary Figure 1A).
In addition, five short-term screens were performed on pediatric patient-derived
non-malignant tissue, including fibroblasts (n = 2), astrocytes (n = 2), and

Chapter 386
PBMCs (n = 1). The feasibility of the different approaches was assessed by
comparing establishment timelines and success rates (defined as successful
culture establishment and high-quality drug screen). Short-term screens of both
patient and PDX material provided drug sensitivity profiles within 14 days of
sample receipt, whereas organoid models required 3-12 months. In the KiTZ
cohort, patient-derived short-term screens were successfully established and
performed in 31% of cases, whereas patient-derived organoid establishment
succeeded in 13% of attempts. The short-term screens from patient-derived non-
malignant tissue were successful in 86% of attempts (one failed quality control).
Across both cohorts, PDX-derived short-term screens were successfully
established in 78% of attempts, compared with 27% for PDX-derived organoids.
Most short-term screen failures were due to insufficient viable cell yield prior to
plating and all organoid failures were caused by growth arrest at long-term
culture. Of note, four screens were excluded from further analyses due to murine
content (n = 2) or because they represented duplicate screens from the same
patient (n = 2). 15 These results show that both the turnaround times and success
rates of short-term screens are superior to organoid screens, indicating that
short-term screens could be more suitable for real-time clinical decision making.
To interpret drug sensitivity profiles in a molecular context, we analyzed whole
exome sequencing, RNA sequencing and methylation array on patient tumors,
PDX tumors, and the organoid models for which drug screens were performed in
the Máxima. The most frequent molecular events were MYCN amplification, ALK
mutation, loss of chromosome 1p, loss of chromosome 11q, and gain of
chromosome 17q (Supplementary Figure 1B). To determine if PDX and organoid
models retain the genetic alterations of the originating patient tumor, we
examined driver events in models where tumor data was available. In matched
samples, all driver events were maintained with the exception of a chromosome
1p loss observed in the NB0211 patient tumor but absent in the PDX and organoid
models (Fig. 1C). We also assessed whether gene expression patterns were
consistent for organoids in the Máxima cohort. We indeed show that models
generally cluster close to the originating tumor (Supplementary Figure 2). These
results demonstrate that neuroblastoma short-term, organoid, and PDX models
can be successfully established while maintaining the key genomic and
phenotypic features of the original patient tumor.

To assess whether drug sensitivity is influenced by in vivo expansion, we
compared drug response of six matched samples, including short-term (n = 4)
and organoid (n = 2) screens from either patient or PDX material (Fig. 2B).
Matched drug response profiles are highly correlated despite differences in
sample origin (mean r = 0.84; Fig. 2C; Supplementary Figure 6; Supplementary
Figure 7A). No drug was significantly associated with origin of the model
indicating that this factor did not have a major influence on drug sensitivity
(Supplementary Figure 7B). These results demonstrate that PDX-derived models
recapitulate drug sensitivity observed in patient-derived material.
To evaluate the influence of the duration of in vitro culturing (max. 7 days
versus 3-12 months), we compared drug sensitivities of matched short-term and
organoid screens (PDX n = 7, patient n = 2). In the Máxima cohort, additional
methodological differences between short-term and organoid screens existed: the
culture medium and the compound incubation time (72 hours versus 120 hours
in the organoids). Despite these differences, short-term and organoid screens
show similar trends in drug response (average Pearson correlation = 0.87; Fig.
2D; Supplementary Figure 7C), and no drugs significantly differed in their
efficacy across the two model systems (Supplementary Figure 7D-E). Next to
consistent drug sensitivities across patient- and PDX-derived tissues, these
results indicate that short-term screens recapitulate drug responses of the
organoids, the current standard for functional profiling, 9,18,19 while shortening the
turnaround from months to days.
Genomic and transcriptomic features in relation to in vitro drug
response
To evaluate whether genomic or transcriptomic features of untreated
neuroblastoma samples are associated with drug sensitivity in short-term and
organoid models, we associated drug response with corresponding molecular
data. When multiple screens of one sample were available, one representative
screen (the short-term PDX-derived screen, available for all these samples) was
included in this analysis. To evaluate whether targetable genetic alterations are
associated with ex vivo drug response, we compared sensitivities in altered versus
wild-type samples. Across the two cohorts, three targetable alterations were
significantly associated with drug response (Fig. 3A; Supplementary Figure 8A).

Chapter 392
Increased sensitivity to MDM2 inhibition was observed in TP53 wild-type
samples compared to homozygous TP53-altered samples, with a significant
association for idasanutlin and XPO1 inhibitor selinexor in the Máxima cohort,
and trends in the same direction in the KiTZ cohort. These findings validate
previous reports of resistance of tumors with a TP53 inactivation to MDM2 and
XPO1 inhibitors.20,21 However, subgroup sizes for these comparisons were small
and these exploratory associations may be driven by a limited number of cases.
Next to this, ALK alterations were significantly associated with sensitivity to ALK
inhibitor lorlatinib in the Máxima cohort, with the same trend in KiTZ, consistent
with the use of ALK status as a biomarker for treatment with lorlatinib.22
However, ALK alterations were not associated with sensitivity to other ALK
inhibitors, which might be due to the limited ALK-altered samples in our dataset.
Other alterations, such as SMARCA4 and MYCN, were not significantly
associated with drug sensitivity in either cohort. Although this should be
validated in larger cohorts, these results indicate that genetic alterations alone
may not be sufficient to predict ex vivo drug sensitivity in neuroblastoma.
To explore whether expression of target genes or pathways reflects drug
sensitivity, drug responses were correlated with RNA expression of each
compound’s known target gene or pathway, where transcriptomic data were
available (3B-C; Supplementary Figure 8B). The strongest correlations included
an association between sensitivity to futibatinib and higher FGFR4 expression
and sensitivity to ribociclib with elevated expression of cell cycle genes (Fig. 3B).
ALK mutational status was associated with lorlatinib sensitivity but not for the
other four ALK inhibitors tested. Next, we explored if transcriptomic features
might provide additional context, by examining ALK expression and activity of
the PI3K-AKT pathway. ALK expression did not correlate significantly with ALK
inhibitor sensitivity, except for entrectinib (Supplementary Figure 8B), driven by
one ALK-amplified sample with elevated ALK expression. Interestingly, reduced
activity of the PI3K-AKT pathway did correlate with increased sensitivity to
ceritinib, alectinib, and lorlatinib (Fig. 3C). The PI3K-AKT pathway functions
downstream of ALK signaling and has been previously reported as a resistance
mechanism.23,24 These exploratory findings suggest that transcriptomic context
may complement mutational status in the investigation of biomarkers of
response.

Drug sensitivity profiling to assess tumor selectivity in
neuroblastoma
To identify if drugs are more effective in tumor or non-malignant cells, we
compared the drug sensitivities of neuroblastoma to patient-derived non-
malignant pediatric samples (fibroblasts (n = 2), astrocytes (n = 2), and PBMCs
(n = 1)) screened at KiTZ. First, we analyzed the compounds comprising the
clinical backbone of high-risk neuroblastoma treatment as used in the SIOPEN
HR-NBL2 trial 25 (Fig. 4A). Cisplatin (p = 0.04) and etoposide (p = 0.19) were
more effective in tumor than non-malignant samples. In contrast, doxorubicin
and vincristine were similarly effective.
To identify tumor-specific drugs, we compared drug sensitivity in tumor and
non-malignant models. Figure 4B shows the 15 most tumor selective drugs.
Besides cisplatin (Fig. 4A), four compounds were significantly more effective in
tumor samples: BCL2 inhibitors navitoclax and venetoclax, MDM2 inhibitor
idasanutlin, and topoisomerase inhibitor mitoxantrone (Fig. 4C). Conversely, we
identified drugs for which non-malignant cells are more sensitive
(Supplementary Figure 9A): MEK inhibitors cobimetinib and trametinib,
tyrosine kinase inhibitor dasatinib, mTOR inhibitors everolimus and
temsirolimus, and HDAC inhibitor panobinostat (Supplementary Figure 9B).
These findings highlight the value of including pediatric non-malignant tissues as
a reference in drug screens to identify compounds with favorable tumor
selectivity and flag those with potential toxicity.

To evaluate concordance between drug sensitivity in ex vivo short-term screens
and therapeutic responses in corresponding PDX models, we compared the ex
vivo AUCs with in vivo tumor volume. Although the assays differ substantially in
design (constant 72-hour exposure across six concentrations ex vivo versus
intermittent dosing of a single concentration over 28 days in vivo), we observed
concordant response patterns for several compounds. Topotecan was highly
effective in both model systems, reducing in vivo tumor volume and ex vivo
viability in most samples (Supplementary Figure 10A-B). In contrast,
belvarafenib was generally not effective in both settings, with high tumor volumes
in vivo (tumor volumes >5) and low ex vivo sensitivity (AUC > 75). As compounds
that are effective for only part of the patients are most relevant for precision
oncology, we assessed sample-level concordance (Fig. 5B; Supplementary Figure
10C). Three drugs showed strong rank-based concordance (spearman ρ > 0.6):
the ALK inhibitor alectinib (ρ = 1), the MEK inhibitor cobimetinib (ρ = 0.71) and
the chromatin-remodeling BET inhibitor JQ-1 (ρ = 0.61). Moderate concordance
was observed for the topoisomerase inhibitor etoposide (ρ = 0.54) and the MDM2
inhibitor idasanutlin (ρ = 0.45). For idasanutlin, most ex vivo responders also
responded in vivo. However, an exception was NB0542, which was resistant in
vivo (tumor volume = 17), despite moderate ex vivo sensitivity (AUC = 76, slightly
above the mean of 72) – consistent with its TP53 wild-type status. Weak
concordance (ρ < 0.4) is found for three compounds: copanlisib, prexasertib and
lorlatinib. Overall, these findings demonstrate encouraging in vivo concordance
for seven out of ten drugs tested.
Discussion
Despite intensive treatment, survival of high-risk neuroblastoma patients
remains around 50%. Molecular profiling alone is insufficient to stratify
treatment for all patients. 12,26–28 Functional profiling using organoids and
patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models has shown promise but is limited by
establishment timelines and success rates.9,11,12 Here, we evaluated the suitability
for precision medicine of three types of patient-derived neuroblastoma models:
the short-term cultures, organoids, and PDX models. We performed 55 drug
screens on tissues derived from 38 neuroblastoma patients and 5 non-malignant

across preclinical neuroblastoma models1013
samples. In parallel ten compounds were tested in vivo, in eight neuroblastoma
PDX models.17 Short-term drug screens achieved higher success rates and
shortened establishment times compared to organoids while retaining the drug
response profiles. Short-term screens also showed encouraging concordance with
in vivo PDX model treatment response for seven out of ten compounds tested.
PDX models remain widely used in neuroblastoma to enable in vivo assessment
of drug efficacy and tolerability. 8,9 In our study, PDX models retained the major
genetic and transcriptomic characteristics of their originating tumors. However,
their suitability for personalized precision medicine is constrained by low
engraftment success, high costs and long establishment times. 29,30 Moreover,
treatment responses in PDXs do not always fully mirror patient activity or
toxicity, as murine pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics differ from those
in children.29,30 In addition, the use of animals raises ethical considerations, and
regulatory agencies such as the FDA increasingly encourage alternatives to
animal-based preclinical testing. 31 These limitations motivate the search for
alternative patient-derived model systems that are eligible for precision
medicine.
We compared four different ex vivo drug screening approaches and observed
concordance in the responses of short-term and organoid screens, as well as
between drug screens derived from patient material and those derived from PDX.
Although this cohort was enriched for MYCN-amplified tumors due to the
availability of matched PDX models with corresponding in vivo drug response
data, it enabled direct comparison of ex vivo and in vivo drug responses. To the
best of our knowledge, such cross-model comparisons have rarely been
systematically explored. Previous work from the ZERO program also
demonstrated strong concordance between short term screens of matched
patient- and PDX-derived tissue for a single rhabdomyosarcoma case.13 Our study
extends on these observations and provides a unique dataset which allows direct
comparison of drug responses before and after in vitro and/or in vivo expansion.
Organoid models can be derived from both patient samples and from PDX
models. Organoids are attractive for large-scale drug discovery and mechanistic

Chapter 3102
studies. In our study, patient-derived organoids were successfully established in
only 13% of attempts, while PDX-derived organoids achieved a success rate of
27%. In contrast, patient-derived short-term cultures succeeded in 31% of
attempts and PDX-derived short-term cultures in 78%. The lower success rates
for patient samples are likely reflecting the limited amount and variable quality
of material obtained directly from patient samples. The turnaround time for
organoid establishment and screening was 3-12 months, and similar timelines
have been reported by others for neuroblastoma organoid models.9,10,32 These
timelines often exceed the median progression-free survival of relapsed or high-
risk patients (4 – 7 months), which restricts their use for real-time clinical
decision making. 11 A second potential downside is clonal selection during
prolonged culture. Karlsson et al.32 demonstrated that within 42 days (11
passages), the major subclone can expand to fixation while others are lost. Such
evolution over months of culture may influence drug responses by not fully
reflecting the polyclonal composition of the tumor. Short-term cultures are likely
better preserving the cellular and clonal composition of the original tumor,
although quantification of compositional drift was not performed in this study.14
Overall, these factors limit the suitability of organoids for real-time clinical
decision making.
Ex vivo short-term cultures offer a faster approach for preclinical drug testing. In
our study, patient-derived short-term screens were successfully established in
31% of cases, whereas PDX-derived short-term screens achieved a success rate of
78%. Ex vivo short-term screens can support precision medicine, by identifying
patient-specific drug sensitivities, although prospective clinical studies are
required to establish their predictive value for patient response. 15 Although
treatment decisions were not based on the drug screening results generated in
this study, previous work from ZERO and INFORM demonstrated the feasibility
of integrating ex vivo short-term screens cultures in precision medicine programs
as the rapid turnaround time allows integration into multidisciplinary tumor
boards. 13,14 The integration of molecular and functional data may provide a higher
level of clinical confidence in treatment recommendations. In ZERO, 82% of
screens were completed while patients were still alive. In addition, in INFORM,
we observed preservation of the tumor microenvironment (with a trend for tumor

across preclinical neuroblastoma models1033
cell enrichment) during preculture and drug screening. As short-term cultures
can retain residual microenvironmental cells, they may provide a more
representative tumor model than long-term models. To account for residual
microenvironment cells, future studies should develop methods to distinguish
between tumor and non-tumor cells to determine the tumor-specific drug
response. The inclusion of the tumor microenvironment may enable testing of
clinically relevant immunotherapies such as anti-GD2 antibodies. In contrast, the
evaluation of anti-angiogenic agents is not feasible in this system. In addition,
further optimizing success rates and reducing the required cell numbers per well
will be essential for implementation of drug screening when using small needle
biopsies.
To assess whether ex vivo drug responses correspond with in vivo activity, we
compared ex vivo drug sensitivity from short-term screens with matched PDX
model responses, performed within the ITCC-P4 consortium. 16,17 We observed
encouraging concordance with in vivo PDX models for seven agents, including
kinase inhibitors targeting ALK (alectinib), MEK (cobimetinib) and MDM2
inhibitor idasanutlin. For others (e.g. copanlisib), concordance was limited,
which could be due to several factors. Direct comparisons are constrained by
major differences between the models, such as discordant drug concentrations,
treatment durations, and pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters.33
For rapidly metabolized compounds, ex vivo concentrations may be higher than
concentrations achievable in plasma or tumor tissue, which may explain the lack
of in vivo efficacy even when ex vivo sensitivity is observed. Another potential
difference is the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo growth rates, which
especially impacts sensitivity to cytotoxic agents 34,35. Besides these differences, in
vivo models are known for their biological variability in treatment response.36
Therefore, using an n-of-1 setup limits our direct comparison between in vivo and
ex vivo sensitivity. Lastly, the PDXs tested in vivo were not from the same passage
from which the ex vivo models were derived, introducing the possibility of clonal
shifts between the passages. Ultimately though, direct correlation with in-patient,
not PDX, response holds clinical value. Future studies with larger, clinically
annotated cohorts should investigate whether prior treatment exposure results in
resistance to the same agents in ex vivo drug screens. Previous work by ZERO13

Chapter 3104
and INFORM14 demonstrated that ex vivo sensitivities were consistent with
responses in matched PDXs and, critically, in patients.
Beyond predicting tumor response, functional assays may also provide insights
into potential tumor selectivity and toxicity. Two of the clinical backbone agents
used in high-risk neuroblastoma treatment, doxorubicin and vincristine, showed
comparable effectiveness in neuroblastoma and patient-derived non-malignant
samples. This is consistent with previous reports of doxorubicin-related
cardiotoxicity and vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy. 37,38 In our study,
topotecan, navitoclax, venetoclax and idasanutlin were significantly more
effective in tumor than non-malignant samples. Consistent with these findings,
clinical studies report tolerability with promising clinical outcomes for topotecan,
navitoclax and venetoclax in neuroblastoma or other pediatric solid tumors. 39–43
Interestingly, topotecan also demonstrated high efficacy in both ex vivo and in
vivo models. Although idasanutlin showed more efficacy in tumor than non-
malignant samples, a phase I trial of idasanutlin in patients with leukemias or
solid tumors was terminated due to toxicity and lack of efficacy. 44 In addition,
some compounds were more effective in non-malignant cells than in tumor cells.
This may reflect the dependence of non-malignant proliferating cells and
immune cells on the targeted pathways. For dasatinib, PBMCs specifically
showed the highest sensitivity, consistent with the known dependence of
lymphocytes on Src-family kinase signaling for T-cell activation and
proliferation.45,46 For MEK inhibitors cobimetinib and trametinib,
neuroblastoma cells in our cohort could be less dependent on RAS-MEK-ERK
signaling than non-malignant proliferating cells, and/or may have acquired
bypass mechanisms that further reduce single-agent sensitivity. For mTOR
inhibitors , a clinical trial combining temsirolimus with re-induction
chemotherapy reported excessive toxicity in children with relapsed acute
lymphoblastic leukemia. 47 However, interpretation is limited by the small sample
size for non-malignant samples. In addition, this analysis considered all tumor
samples collectively, irrespective of genetic or transcriptomic features, and all
non-malignant samples irrespective of tissue origin. The non-malignant samples
used in this study were selected based on the feasibility of obtaining pediatric
samples through minimally invasive procedures. They provide an initial reference
for evaluating tumor selectivity, but do not represent the major organs involved

across preclinical neuroblastoma models1053
in drug metabolism or dose-limiting toxicity. Future studies should focus on
establishing larger reference panels including pediatric liver, kidney, and
intestine tissues. 48–51 Including non-malignant pediatric tissues in ex vivo drug
screening may help identify drugs that could cause unacceptable toxicity.
Another possible advantage of collecting a large non-malignant panel is that it
allows the investigation of how inherited genetic variation influences drug
toxicity. This is particularly relevant in neuroblastoma, where young survivors
face long-term treatment-related risks of (cardiovascular) complications and
secondary malignancies.52
In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that drug sensitivities were generally
consistent between short-term and organoid screens, but these models differ
markedly in feasibility and turnaround times. Prospective clinical studies will be
essential to determine whether ex vivo drug responses predict patient response.
Additionally, future studies should extend single-agent screens to include
validated drug combinations. While organoids and PDX models remain essential
for large-scale drug discovery and biomarkers research, ex vivo short-term
screening offers higher success rates and rapid establishment times, making it
well suited to complement molecular profiling for precision oncology in
neuroblastoma and possibly other pediatric and adult tumors.

ITCC-P4 drug screen in PDX for response characterization
ITCC-P4 PDX models were characterized for their response to single compound
or combination therapies in preclinical single-mouse trials.16,17 Based on
individual formulation and specific schedules, single compounds and
combinations were administered either orally, intravenously, subcutaneously, or
intraperitoneally (Table 1). When the PDX tumor volume achieves a size of 100-
250 mm³, a blinded randomization procedure was used to distribute mice to test
groups with the subsequent start of treatment. The actual amount of compound
was calculated daily depending on the individual body weight of animals
throughout a four-cycle 28-day treatment phase. All animals were terminated at
individual time points when they reached the maximum ethical tumor volume
threshold (TV > 1.5cm³), body weight loss (>20%) limits, or when animals
suffered from adverse effects before the end of four cycles. Control animals
receive the most demanding schedule and therefore the lorlatinib vehicle
formulation. From the first treatment day onwards, tumor size is measured twice
a week until the end of the treatment.
Tissue dissociation
PDX-derived tumor tissue (both cohorts) and patient-derived tumor tissue
(KiTZ) were processed using a site-specific enzymatic digestion protocol. Tissue
was incubated in Liberase DL (Sigma Aldrich, cat. no. 5466202001; 1:43 dilution)
in tumor stem media (TSM) 14 at 37°C for 30 minutes with occasional swirling
(Máxima) or in trypsin (10 mg/ml) at 37°C for ten minutes (KiTZ). TSM consists
of 47.5% Neurobasal-A medium, 47.5% D-MEM/F-12, 1% HEPES buffer solution
(1 M), 1% sodium pyruvate MEM (100 mM, CE), 1% MEM non-essential amino
acids solution (10 mM), L-glutamine solution BIOXTRA (2 mM), and 1%
penicillin-streptomycin-glutamine (all from Life Technologies, Thermo Fisher
Scientific Inc.). This was supplemented with 2% B27 Supplement Minus Vitamin
A (50×; Life Technologies, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, MA, USA),
0.02% (w/v) recombinant human EGF (100 μg/mL), 0.02% (w/v) recombinant
human FGF-basic (100 μg/mL), 0.05% H-PDGF-AA (20 μg/mL) (all from
PeproTech Inc., Rocky Hill, NJ, USA), and 0.1% heparin solution (2 mg/mL;
Sigma-Aldrich, Munich, Germany). Enzymatic activity was stopped by harvesting
the supernatant, adding medium (Máxima), or by adding 12 μl trypsin inhibitor,

followed by repeated additions of a 1:1 mixture of 1 M MgCl 2 and DNase (2
mg/mL; 60 μL per addition) until the tumor fragment settles (KiTZ). At the
Máxima, the residual tissue underwent a second digestion in Liberase TM (Sigma
Aldrich, cat. no. 5401119001; 1:43 dilution in TSM). After another 30 minutes,
cells were harvested as described above. Cells were filtered through a pre-washed
70 μm cell strainer (Máxima) or a 70- or 100 μm strainer (KiTZ) and centrifuged
at 300 g for 5 minutes (Máxima) or at 400-500 g for 10 minutes (KiTZ). Red
blood cells were lysed using lysis buffer with a maximum incubation time of 2-5
minutes at room temperature. Cells were resuspended in TSM complete 14 and
counted using trypan blue.
Short- and long-term organoid culture
After tumor tissue dissociation, cells were cultured for short-term or until
organoids were established. In all cases, tumor cells were cultured at 37°C, 5%
CO₂. Short-term cultures and screens at the Máxima and KiTZ were done in TSM.
At the Princess Máxima Center, DNA was harvested before drug screening.
Freshly dissociated cells were cultured for 5-8 days (at Máxima) or for 2-7 days
(depending on growth and morphology, at KiTZ), before screening. Two short-
term screens were excluded due to mice contamination.
Long-term organoid cultures at the Máxima were cultured in Neuroblastoma
Organoid Medium (NBOM), consisting of DMEM with GlutaMAX™ (Life
Technologies, cat. no. 21885108), 25% Ham’s F-12 Nutrient Mix, B-27™
Supplement (minus vitamin A), N-2 Supplement, 100 U/mL penicillin, 100
μg/mL streptomycin, 20 ng/mL recombinant human EGF, 40 ng/mL
recombinant human FGF-basic, 200 ng/mL recombinant human IGF-I, 10
ng/mL recombinant human PDGF-AA, and 10 ng/mL recombinant human
PDGF-BB. 55 At KiTZ, long-term cultures were cultured in TSM. In both centers,
cells were cultured biweekly, with medium refreshment or passaging based on
microscopic evaluation. Medium was refreshed by harvesting medium,
centrifuging at 250 g for 5 minutes, and resuspending the pellet in fresh medium.
Oversized cultures with necrotic cores were dissociated by pipetting in a 50 mL
tube before splitting (Máxima) or using Trypl Express (Life Technologies,
Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, MA, USA; 5 min, 37 °C; KiTZ).
Mycoplasma testing and STR profiling (PowerPlex system and GeneMapper

Chapter 3110
software, Promega) were performed routinely. Drug screening of long-term
organoid cultures was initiated only after stable growth of human tumor cells was
confirmed. Tumor content was confirmed by comparing patient-specific
breakpoints of the culture (using SNP array) to those of the original tumor. On
the day of organoid screening, cryovials, RNA, and DNA were harvested at the
Máxima. For all organoid models established at KiTZ, unsupervised clustering of
genome-wide DNA methylation data (Illumina 850K array) was performed, using
t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) to confirm clustering of the
long-term culture with the original fresh frozen sample of the patient and with
the appropriate reference methylation classes. Concordance of key molecular
alterations is additionally assessed by direct comparison of CNA profiles derived
from the same methylation array datasets between patient-derived fresh frozen
samples and matched organoid models.
Part of the KiTZ short-term screens were previously reported in Peterziel et
al.14, Máxima organoids from patient material were previously reported in
Langenberg et al.9, and Máxima short-term screens on ex vivo cultures from PDX
models were previously reported. 15,56
Molecular profiling
For models used for drug screening in the Máxima, comprehensive molecular
profiling was performed as part of the ITCC-P4 consortium 16,17 in Paris (Curie)
and Heidelberg (KiTZ), on PDX and organoid samples, and if available, on
primary patient tumors and matched germline controls. For models used for drug
screening at KiTZ, genome sequencing was exclusively performed on the primary
patient tumor. For low-coverage whole-genome sequencing (lcWGS) and whole-
exome sequencing (WES), libraries were prepared using standardized methods 27
and captured with the Agilent SureSelect Clinical Research Exome V2 Kit,
followed by sequencing using Illumina platforms at both centers. For PDX
models, organoids and, if available, primary patient tumors, used for drug
screening at Máxima, RNA-seq was also performed by the ITCC-P4
consortium 16,17 in Paris (Curie) and Heidelberg (KiTZ). RNA-seq was performed
on the NextSeq 500 (150 nt paired-end) or NovaSeq (100 nt paired-end).

Drug libraries
The Máxima drug libraries L13 and L14 consist of 224 and 226 drugs,
respectively, including FDA-approved agents and those in (pre-)clinical
development (Supplementary Table 1). All organoids are screened with the full
library. For short-term screens, the full library is used when sufficient biomass is
available; otherwise, the clinical subset of 134 drugs is used. The KiTZ drug
library consists of 78 clinically relevant anticancer drugs, including targeted as
well as chemotherapy (Supplementary Table 1). Both libraries consist of clinically
relevant anticancer drugs, including FDA-approved agents and those in (pre-)
clinical development. Most drugs are dissolved in DMSO and stored under
nitrogen at room temperature (Máxima) or in an oxygen- and moisture-free
environment at room temperature (KiTZ). At the Máxima, exceptions include five
drugs (metformin, perifosine, carboplatin, oxaliplatin, and copanlisib) dissolved
in MQ, and cisplatin in saline, which are stored at –20 °C. Before screening, 384-
well working plates (Labcyte 384LDV) are shaken (30 min at room temperature)
and centrifuged (2.5 min at 1500 rpm). The Echo 550 dispenser is then used to
verify well volume (>2.5 μL) and DMSO percentage (>80%).
Drug screening
Drug screens were performed in duplicate. Cells (5,000/well in 40 μL at the
Máxima; 1000/well in 25 μL at KiTZ) were plated into 384-well flat-bottom tissue
culture plates (#3764, Corning) using a multidrop combi dispenser (Thermo
Scientific) and cultured for 24 hours (Máxima) or directly screened (KiTZ, as
described in Peterziel et al.14). At the Máxima, cell viability was assessed at t = 0
using the Cell Titer Glo 3D (CTG3D) assay (Promega, G9683) according to the
manufacturer's protocol.
Using the Echo 550, 100 nL of each drug (in DMSO or MQ) was added to
achieve final concentrations ranging from 0.1 nM to 100 μM (0.25% DMSO/MQ).
DMSO-only treated cells served as negative controls; 10 μM staurosporine-
treated cells were used as positive controls. Cells were incubated with the drugs
for 72 hours at 37°C and 5% CO₂, except for organoid screens at the Máxima (120
hours).
Data were normalized against DMSO-treated (100% viability) and empty well
controls (0% viability). Dose-response curves were modeled using a five-

Chapter 3112
parameter log-logistic model with the R package drc (v3.0.1; R 4.3.1 57). From
these models, the IC50 (concentration for 50% viability reduction), area under
the curve (AUC), and relative cell growth (Máxima, CTG3D signal day 5/t0) were
calculated. Screen quality was assessed based on growth dynamics, control
performance, and consistency across replicates. At the Máxima, a screen was
considered successful if: (1) clear separation was observed between staurosporine
(positive control) and DMSO (vehicle control) responses; (2) relative cell growth
exceeded 60% over the assay duration; and (3) replicate consistency and
individual dose-response curves passed independent visual inspection by two
researchers. For PDX-derived short-term screens at the Máxima, tumor cell
content was additionally verified at the time of screening using qPCR
quantification of human versus murine cell proportions.15 Cell viabilities prior to
screening were 80–97% across both patient- and PDX-derived short-term and
organoid screens. At KiTZ, screen quality was assessed using a Robust Z-score
approach based on DMSO and benzylamine nucleoside controls, yielding high-
and medium-quality screens; for medium-quality screens, replicate correlation
and raw signal strength were additionally evaluated, as previously described.14
Establishment success was defined as the successful generation of a culture of
which a drug screen that passed the predefined quality-control criteria could be
performed. AUC was the primary metric used for defining and comparing drug
sensitivities, as IC50 could not be reliably determined for inactive drugs. We
normalized the area under the curve (AUC) between 0-100, accounting for
differences in the number of concentrations across cohorts.
Calling of genomic alterations
Whole-exome sequencing was used to identify genomic alterations as described
above. High-level amplifications of MYCN, ALK, CDK4, KRAS, and MDM2 were
called when copy number (CN) > 8. ALK alterations were also called in case of an
activating mutation within the tyrosine kinase domain. Alterations in genes
TERT, NF1, PTPN11, PIK3CA, CDKN2A/B and AKT were considered based on
homozygous deletions, or loss of heterozygosity (LOH) in combination with an
inactivating mutation. ATRX was called in case of homozygous inactivation or
deletion, or the combination of LOH, in-frame fusions, inactivating mutations, or
hotspot mutations. TP53 mutations were called in case of a deletion combined

with an inactivating (frameshift or SNV) mutation. Chromosomal gains were
called when CN > 2.5 and losses when CN < 1.5.
RNA-sequencing normalization and gene set enrichment
RNA-sequencing data were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh37,
GENCODE 19) using STAR 58 and the raw counts were normalized to CPM values
using the Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) method implemented in the
edgeR59 R package (version 4.6.2) and log2 transformed. Gene set scores were
calculated using GSVA60 (version 2.2.0) and gene sets were obtained from the
Reactome database.61
Statistical testing
Statistical analysis was performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.62 Correlation
was calculated using Pearson correlation 63 (package stats, version 3.6.2) to assess
linear relationships. For in vivo-ex vivo comparison, Spearman concordance was
used. P-values were used to evaluate the statistical significance of the observed
correlations. Differential response analysis between tissue sources and models was
performed using Limma64 (version 3.21). To correct for multiple hypothesis testing,
p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg65 method. Significance was
considered when the p-value was below 0.05.

Chapter 4132
Abstract
Background. Neuroblastoma is among the most fatal pediatric solid tumors and
high-risk patients face poor survival despite intensive treatment. Genomic
profiling alone has not translated into effective treatment stratification for all
neuroblastoma patients. Drug screening offers a complementary strategy, but
conventional preclinical models are constrained by limited establishment success
from low-input material and by timelines often incompatible with diagnostic
decision-making. Here, we evaluated MicroOrganoSphere (MOS) technology,
in which tumor cells are encapsulated in Matrigel droplets generated by
microfluidic droplet formation, by a head-to-head comparison with the
conventional suspension cultures to improve growth and drug testing in
neuroblastoma.
Methods. MOS were established from patient-derived tumoroids, freshly
dissociated patient-derived xenograft (PDX) tumors, PDX-derived tumoroids,
and a freshly dissociated patient tumor to compare growth and drug responses
with suspension.
Results. Tumor cell growth in MOS was comparable or superior to suspension
cultures. MOS drug screens were performed at a 2.5-fold lower seeding density
compared to suspension, whilst maintaining reliable results with consistent drug
sensitivity profiles and screen quality to suspension. Promisingly, drug testing in
MOS was feasible within 9 days of receiving fresh PDX tumor tissue.
Conclusion. These results demonstrate in a proof-of-concept setting how
MOS technology could support the establishment and drug screening of
neuroblastoma cultures from low-input samples within clinically relevant
timelines. MOS technology provides a promising functional platform to
accelerate preclinical drug testing in neuroblastoma precision medicine.
Keywords: precision medicine, 3D cancer models, pediatric oncology,
neuroblastoma.

Introduction
Neuroblastoma, the most prevalent pediatric extra-cranial solid tumor, poses a
therapeutic challenge [1]. Current treatment for high-risk patients includes
induction chemotherapy, surgery, high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem
cell transplantation and radiation therapy followed by consolidation therapy with
anti-GD2 antibody treatment and retinoic acid [2]. Despite their rigorous
treatment regimen, high risk patients face a 5-year overall survival of 50% [3].
The heterogeneity in clinical response highlights the urgent need for a more
effective and targeted approach. Median progression-free survival across high-
risk pediatric cancers, including neuroblastoma, has been reported as 116 days
[4] with ranges from 1-65 months reported for neuroblastoma patients [5]. This
emphasizes the limited clinical window for identification of effective therapeutic
strategies.
Currently, pediatric precision oncology trials use genome sequencing to identify
patient-specific targetable driver mutations to guide clinical decisions [4,6]. Such
actionable driver genes are detected in 37-94% of patients, and the clinical benefit
from matched targeted therapies remains limited for many patients. This can
partly be explained as genetic characterization does not fully capture the disease’s
complexity, and epigenetic and microenvironmental factors should also be
considered [7,8]. As an alternative screening approach that could overcome these
limitations, functional drug testing is increasingly considered to guide treatment
[8–14]. In vivo patient derived xenograft (PDX) models are representative and
have been used extensively to study tumor response [15]. However, they are low-
throughput, time-consuming and expensive to develop and maintain, as
engraftment and stable expansion require approximately 1-11 months, followed
by several weeks to assess drug response [9,16–18]. While 2D cell lines are easy
to culture, they fail to mimic the tumor's complex architecture [16]. 3D patient-
derived tumoroids, that have been established for neuroblastoma [10,18,19], offer
a more promising middle ground with better scalability and lower costs compared
to PDX. They more accurately mimic the architecture and physiological responses
of solid tumors compared to 2D models [20]. However, tumoroid establishment
has several limitations that hinder its clinical implementation for precision
medicine: the required large amount of input material, limited success rate, loss

Chapter 4134
of the tumor microenvironment and extended establishment time, typically
requiring 3-12 months, after which drug testing typically lasts 5 days [4,9,10,12–
14,16,18,20,21]. This often exceeds patients’ progression-free survival [4].
Patients are treated during these extended establishment periods of PDX and
tumoroid models, which may limit the representation of the current state of the
patient’s tumor. Additionally, in precision oncology programs, treatment
strategies are typically discussed in a Molecular Tumor Board, where molecular
profiling results become available after a mean turnaround time of 25.4 days. To
allow integrated discussion alongside molecular profiling, preclinical models
used to guide treatment decisions should ideally provide drug response
predictions within a similar timeframe. To shorten establishment timelines, ex
vivo short-term drug screening can be performed on freshly dissociated tumor
tissue cultured in suspension. This method has been successfully explored in
novel pediatric precision medicine studies [8,9,11,22], but is limited by the low
quantity of available tumor material from minimally invasive procedures used in
children, variable viability after dissociation, and the time required to expand
sufficient biomass prior to screening. Further optimization is therefore required
to improve success rates and reduce the time to screen.
MicroOrganoSphere (MOS) technology can be used to overcome the
previously mentioned limitations of ex vivo screens. MOS are droplets
generated by microfluidic droplet formation that encapsulate patient-derived
tumor cells in Matrigel. MOS are automatically and rapidly generated from
minimal patient tissue (i.e. low input samples with limited cell numbers) in a
high-throughput fashion [23]. Compared to conventional tumoroids, MOS
require lower input tissue and can be rapidly used for drug screening for
personalized medicine. In colorectal cancer, MOS responses to
chemotherapeutics correlated with clinical outcome [24,25] and Ding et al.
demonstrated that drug sensitivities could be obtained within ~10 days from
small, 18-gauge, biopsies. In addition, MOS accurately recapitulate patient
samples and their microenvironment [24], recapitulate the heterogeneity within
tumors [25] and facilitate the testing of immuno-oncology therapies [26]. The
feasibility of MOS in pediatric solid tumors, with a different developmental
origin and tumor biology than adult colorectal cancer, and its performance

MicroOrganoSphereTM technology to advance drug
screening in neuroblastoma precision medicine1354
relative to suspension cultures have not yet been evaluated. If using MOS
technology in neuroblastoma could reduce the number of cells required per well,
it would allow testing of a broader array of therapeutic agents, increasing the
throughput of drug screening processes with the same biomass input.
In this study, we explore the potential of the MOS platform as an alternative
to previously optimized suspension cultures for neuroblastoma patient-derived
models: patient-derived tumoroids, PDX-derived fresh tumor and tumoroid
models, and a fresh patient tumor. We directly compare MOS and suspension
cultures to assess viability, proliferation and drug sensitivity testing of tumoroids
and freshly dissociated samples. Our findings demonstrate how MOS
technology can support short-term culture and functional drug testing, providing
a framework for integrating MOS into preclinical testing pipelines for
neuroblastoma to overcome some of the key limitations of currently available
technologies.
Methods
Detailed experimental procedures, including model generation, culture
conditions, imaging settings and data processing pipelines, are provided in the
Supplementary Methods.
Model generation and culture
All cultures were maintained at 37°C and 5% CO 2. Tumoroid cultures were
passaged twice per week, routinely tested for Mycoplasma and authenticated by
short tandem repeat profiling.
Patient derived tumoroid cultures
In brief, three patient-derived tumoroids with distinct molecular backgrounds
were selected for outgrowth experiments (Suppl. Table 1) and cultured in
neuroblastoma organoid medium (NBOM) [10,19].
PDX-derived fresh and tumoroid cultures
Neuroblastoma PDX models were previously established and genetically
profiled in the ITCC-P4 consortium [27]. Previously reported comprehensive
molecular profiling was used in this study: low coverage whole genome
sequencing, whole exome sequencing, DNA methylation profiling and RNA

Chapter 4136
sequencing [22,27]. The dissociation method for the PDX samples and the
established PDX tumoroids are previously described [18,22]. In brief, fresh PDX
tumors were mechanically dissociated, followed by a two-step enzymatic
digestion. Fresh PDX cultures were resuspended and cultured in NBOM, with the
exception of NB0026, that was cultured in suspension in TSM for 8 days prior to
drug screening. For tumoroid establishment, freshly dissociated cells were
cultured until stable growth was observed and human tumor cultures were
confirmed by SNP analysis and, subsequently, tumoroids were molecularly
profiled [18].
Patient-derived fresh primary culture
A fresh neuroblastoma tumor sample was obtained during surgical resection of
a refractory patient through an institutionally approved biobank study at the
Princess Máxima Center (PMCLAB2025.660). All procedures were performed in
accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, with age-appropriate written
informed consent from patients and/or parents. Preparation of the tumor pieces
was started within 2 hours after surgery. The primary tumor sample was
dissociated via the Liberase protocol, as described in the Supplementary
Methods, and immediately MOS were generated, and MOS and suspension
cultures were plated in NBOM.
Generation and plating of MicroOrganoSpheresTM
MOS were generated as previously described [24]. Briefly, dissociated tumor
cells from patient-derived tumoroids, PDX and human primary tissue digest
were resuspended in ice-cold, growth factor–reduced Matrigel (Corning) at a
defined density corresponding to 50 viable tumor cells per MOS. The cell–
Matrigel mixture was kept on ice to prevent premature polymerization. MOS
were generated using a proprietary droplet-based microfluidic generator, which
produces highly uniform Matrigel droplets encapsulating tumor cells. Briefly,
the cell–Matrigel suspension was loaded into a temperature-controlled
microfluidic system in which pressure-driven flow generates monodisperse
droplets in an immiscible oil phase. Generation was performed under cooled
conditions to maintain Matrigel in liquid state during droplet formation.
Droplet size is defined by the microfluidic geometry and pressure settings,

MicroOrganoSphereTM technology to advance drug
screening in neuroblastoma precision medicine1374
resulting in reproducible MOS diameters of 230-250 μm. Following droplet
generation, MOS were collected and incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes to allow
Matrigel polymerization. After gelation, solidified MOS were demulsified by
transfer onto a hydrophobic PVDF membrane to separate the oil phase from the
aqueous droplets. After 2–3 minutes, polymerized MOS were recovered using
pre-warmed NBOM. Recovered MOS were counted, centrifuged at 150xg for
5min and subsequently resuspended at the appropriate density for plating for
downstream applications.
Plating of MOS and suspension cultures
For MOS cultures, MOS were dispensed in a 384-well flat bottom plate
(6007460, Perkin Elmer) at a density of 40 MOS per well, final cell density:
2,000 cells per well in 40 μL. For suspension cultures, 40 μL of single cell
suspensions were plated in a flat bottom 384-well tissue culture treated
microplate (#3764, Corning). For cell growth experiments (Fig. 1), 2,000 cells per
well were plated, matching MOS conditions. For drug screening (Fig. 2), the
suspension cultures were seeded at 5,000 cells per well, based on previously
optimized conditions for neuroblastoma drug screening [10,18].
Microscopy-based cell viability readout and analyses
In brief, cell viability was assessed by microscopy using Calcein AM viability dye
(Calcein; 0.625 μM; #65-0853-78, ThermoFisher) and Ethidium-Homodimer-2
(EthD; 2.5 μM; #E3599, ThermoFisher). The readout was performed with either
ImageXpress® Micro Confocal High-Content Imaging system (IXM, Molecular
Devices) or the Thunder Widefield Fluorescence microscope (Thunder, Leica™;
Suppl. Table 1). Wells without any detected viability (<4%) were excluded from
analysis. Image analysis was performed using threshold-based segmentation of
live (Calcein-positive) and dead (EthD-positive) objects, after which integrated
fluorescence intensities were used for downstream analysis.
Drug screening
In brief, drug screening was performed using libraries of 45–90 compounds.
Compounds were tested in duplicate across six concentrations (0.1 nM to 10 μM).

Chapter 4138
DMSO-treated wells served as negative controls and staurosporine-treated wells
as positive controls. Cells were incubated with compounds for 72 hours in fresh
PDX screens and 120 hours in PDX-derived tumoroid screens.
For MOS™ cultures, viability was determined using the microscopy-based
live/dead readout. A t = 0 plate was included to assess growth during the screen.
Viability was calculated from the relative live and dead fluorescence signals. For
suspension cultures, and for comparison in MOS™ cultures after microscopy,
CellTiter-Glo 3D (CTG) was used as a conventional ATP-based viability readout
[18].
Results
Tumor cell growth in MicroOrganoSpheres is comparable or
superior to growth in conventional suspension culture
To assess MOS technology for neuroblastoma cells, growth of tumor cells
derived from various model systems (patient-derived tumoroid, PDX, patient)
was monitored when grown in MOS and compared to the conventional growth
method: in suspension cultures (Fig. 1A). Tumor tissue was dissociated into single
cells and encapsulated in Matrigel droplets using microfluidic droplet generation.
After polymerization and demulsification, MOS were cultured under standard
conditions in direct comparison with suspension cultures. The optimal cell
density for cell growth, determined by microscopic inspection, was identified as
50 cells per MOS (Suppl. Fig. 1A). Microfluidic droplet generation produced
uniform MOS with a diameter of 230–250 μm. Spheroids in MOS did not
exceed this size, whereas suspension cultures could form larger spheroids,
although reliable diameter quantification in suspension was limited due to partial
attachment. Growth was observed using fluorescent-based microscopy, where
adapted-threshold based signal intensity of Calcein AM and Ethidium
Homodimer, were used to identify and quantify the amount of live and dead
objects respectively (Suppl. Fig. 1B-C).
Viable biomass of patient-derived tumoroids cultured in MOS versus
suspension was quantified over eight days. MOS cultures could successfully be
established from all tested patient-derived tumoroids (n = 3), where a biomass
increase was observed over time in all models (Fig. 1B-C; Suppl. Fig. 2A).

MicroOrganoSphereTM technology to advance drug
screening in neuroblastoma precision medicine1394
MaxNB067 demonstrated superior biomass expansion in MOS cultures
compared to suspension, while AMC691B and AMC691T showed comparable
growth in both conditions. Interestingly, AMC691B cells formed more defined 3D
structures in MOS compared to the flatter 2D structures when cultured in
suspension (Fig. 1C). These results show comparable to improved cell growth in
MOS versus suspension cultures derived from patient-derived tumoroids.
Next, MOS cultures were established from freshly dissociated PDX-derived
tissues. PDX-expanded tumors provide sufficient biomass for larger experiments
compared to fresh patient samples, while recapitulating molecular and
phenotypic profiles of the patient tumor [28–30]. Parallel MOS and suspension
cultures were established from four samples and all models showed comparable
viability (Fig. 1D-E; Suppl. Fig. 2B). One model (NB0276) failed to expand in both
conditions, consistent with previous reports describing unsuccessful short-term
neuroblastoma cultures due to failed growth after dissociation [18,22]. To
determine whether possible benefit was due to the presence of Matrigel in the
MOS conditions, and not the MOS themselves, a control experiment with
media enriched with Matrigel was performed. Here, biomass decreased in fresh
PDX cultures enriched with 0.5% and 5% Matrigel compared to NBOM (Suppl.
Fig. 2C). These results indicate that MOS supports cell growth to a similar
extent as suspension in freshly dissociated PDX tissues.
Lastly, for one fresh patient tumor that was available, outgrowth was compared
in MOS versus suspension cultures when established directly from the primary
patient material. Cell growth was monitored over 10 days (Fig. 1F-G). Biomass
rapidly increased in MOS, peaking at day 3, while biomass rapidly decreased in
suspension cultures. These results indicate that MOS technology enables short-
term expansion of fresh patient-derived tumor cells ex vivo. Taken together, these
findings demonstrate that MOS supports viable growth across diverse
neuroblastoma models, including fresh and tumoroid cultures derived from
patients and PDXs.

MicroOrganoSphere technology enables reliable drug screening,
with in vitro drug sensitivities consistent with those obtained using
suspension cultures albeit requiring less biomass
To determine whether MOS cultures can be reliably used for drug sensitivity
testing, automated drug screening in both MOS and suspension culture was
performed on three PDX-derived tumoroid models and one freshly dissociated
PDX sample (Fig. 1A). Drug sensitivity of suspension cultures was assessed using
CTG-based viability, the conventional method for neuroblastoma tumoroid
screens [10]. For MOS cultures, drug sensitivity was evaluated using the
microscopy-based live/dead ratio quantification (Calcein for viable objects, EthD
for dead objects; described in Methods). For each compound tested, six
concentrations were screened in duplicate. Between 45 and 90 compounds were

MicroOrganoSphereTM technology to advance drug
screening in neuroblastoma precision medicine1434
tested per sample, based on the available biomass, and vehicle (0.25% DMSO)
and staurosporine (10 μM) were included as live and dead control, respectively
(Fig. 2A). Abemaciclib, a CDK4/6 inhibitor inducing approximately 50% cell
death in this model (1 μM), was selected as a representative compound to
visualize intermediate drug response between vehicle and positive control.
To compare drug screen quality and reproducibility, the coefficient of variation
(CV) in vehicle-treated control wells and the inter-replicate correlation were
used. Drug screens in MOS cultures displayed identical average CVs of 9% in
vehicle-treated control wells compared to suspension cultures (Fig. 2B), which is
within the preferred acceptance threshold of 10% [31]. Average inter-replicate
correlation (same drug, same concentration, different well in the other plate) was
comparable but lower in MOS conditions (r = 0.83) versus in suspension (r =
0.92; Suppl. Fig. 3A). Although MOS drug screens were seeded at 2,000 cells
per well compared to 5,000 cells per well in suspension cultures, screen quality
metrics were comparable between both conditions. We next explored whether
MOS drug screens reflected expected genotype-associated drug response
patterns. NB0026, the only sample with homozygous TP53 inactivation, showed
limited response to the MDM2 inhibitor idasanutlin, whereas the TP53-wild-type
samples were sensitive (Fig. 2C). This is consistent with prior reports, but this
descriptive observation could not be statistically evaluated because of the limited
cohort size (n = 4) and only one TP53-altered sample was included [32–34].
Similarly, NB0026 harbored an ALK mutation, but due to the limited cohort size,
no association between ALK status and ALK inhibitor sensitivity could be
assessed (Suppl. Fig. 3B). Drug response was consistent between MOS and
suspension cultures for three PDX-derived tumoroids and one freshly dissociated
PDX (r = 0.88-0.93; Fig. 2D-E; Suppl. Fig. 3C). To assess whether MOS
conditions affect response of individual compounds, we performed a comparative
analysis between MOS and suspension screens using Limma [35]; adjusted p-
value > 0.05). No individual compound showed a significantly different response
between MOS and suspension cultures. Inclusion of the freshly dissociated PDX
sample NB0026 indicated the ability to rapidly screen low biomass samples. This
sample was briefly cultured in suspension prior to drug screening, which was
performed 9 days after tissue receipt in MOS and suspension, with a 2.5-fold

Chapter 4144
lower seeding density in MOS. These results indicate that, under the conditions
tested here, MOS enables drug screening with comparable drug responses and
screening quality compared to suspension cultures at a 2.5-fold lower seeding
density.
Next to microscopy-based readouts, we used CellTiter-Glo (CTG) luminescent
cell viability assay to determine cell viability and subsequent drug response as this
is the conventional readout for suspension cultures [18,22]. CTG was performed as
a second readout for MOS conditions, on the same wells as the microscopy-based
readout, to assess drug screen quality using CTG as a readout of MOS cultures.
Due to low cell numbers in MOS, CTG readouts were less reliable compared to a
microscopy-based readout. The variability in vehicle-treated control wells was too
high in the CTG-based readout (CV = 0.35, compared to CV = 0.09 in the
microscopy-based readout) and inter-replicate correlation was poor (r = 0.54,
compared to r = 0.83 in the microscopy-based readout; Suppl. Fig. 3D). These
results show that for drug screening in MOS, the microscopy-based readout is a
more reproducible and reliable approach compared to CTG. The microscopy-based
workflow was fully automated and required comparable time to CTG-based
workflows, enabling high-throughput screening. Taken together, these results
show that MOS technology, combined with a microscopy-based readout, enables
reliable drug screening with drug sensitivities and screen quality consistent with
conventional suspension cultures, while using a 2.5-fold lower seeding density.

Discussion
High-risk neuroblastoma remains associated with poor survival despite intense
multimodal treatment, and robust biomarkers for treatment stratification are
lacking in a substantial subset of patients [1,3]. Functional approaches such as in
vitro drug testing have shown promise in guiding treatment in pediatric cancers
[8,9,12,14], but broader implementation is limited by the large amount of
required input material, long turnaround times and low establishment success
[10,12–14,16,21,36]. MicroOrganoSphere (MOS) technology allows for rapid
automated ex vivo testing, with responses to chemotherapy reflecting clinical
outcome [24]. Here, we evaluated the potential of MOS as an alternative for
conventional suspension cultures in neuroblastoma to enable drug screening
from limited cell numbers. By this novel direct comparison, we demonstrate that
MOS technology supports short-term tumor cell growth at least as well as
suspension cultures and that drug screening can be performed using fewer cells
while maintaining reproducibility and drug sensitivity profiles compared to
suspension. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the MOS technology is suitable
for standardized drug screening in the rare and understudied pediatric cancer
neuroblastoma.
Across multiple patient-derived sources, including patient-derived tumoroids,
PDX-derived fresh and tumoroid cultures and one freshly dissociated patient
tumor, MOS supported short-term outgrowth that was comparable or superior
to suspension culture. This data demonstrates that MOS can maintain
neuroblastoma tumor viability even from low-input samples, consistent with
previous work showing successful establishment of MOS cultures from small
18-gauge biopsies [24]. Although only a single primary patient sample could be
included here, this proof-of-concept study supports feasibility for future
expansion to larger patient cohorts. As expected, variability in growth of the
models was observed, especially for the PDX-derived and freshly dissociated
patient tumor. Such variability in growth rates has been previously described and
has been associated with partial failure of model development [18,22].
Drug screening in MOS was performed at 2,000 cells per well compared with
5,000 cells per well in suspension cultures, while maintaining comparable
reproducibility and consistent drug response profiles. The suspension condition

MicroOrganoSphereTM technology to advance drug
screening in neuroblastoma precision medicine1494
reflected the established neuroblastoma drug screening conditions using 5,000
cells per well and a CTG-based viability assessment [18], whereas MOS
screening was optimized for lower-input screening combined with a microscopy-
based viability readout. Potentially a microscopy-based readout could also
improve the quality of suspension drug screens at lower densities. A lower
seeding density allows the same number of compounds to be tested with less
material, which is particularly relevant for fresh patient samples where material
is often limited. While reproducibility of MOS drug screens was comparable to
suspension and below the preferred acceptance threshold of 10% [31,37], well-to-
well variability could be further reduced by quantifying cell viability at the level
of individual MOS rather than at the whole-well level, as applied in this study.
Recent work has demonstrated that single-MOS analyses are feasible and result
in high reproducibility (CV ≤ 2.5; [25]). MOS cultures showed a tendency
toward slightly reduced drug sensitivity compared to suspension, which might be
due to reduced drug penetration into the tumoroids because of the different 3D
structure or the presence of Matrigel. Only for the freshly dissociated PDX sample
NB0026 the effect could be due to presence of tumor micro-environment (TME),
although the trend in this sample is less obvious. Interestingly, the freshly
dissociated patient tumor showed rapid growth in MOS compared to
suspension, where it even decreased in biomass. By testing more samples in the
future, it needs to be investigated whether this large advantage of the MOS
technology is consistent across neuroblastoma subtypes.
In a freshly dissociated PDX sample, MOS drug screening could be
successfully completed within nine days of tissue receipt. Likewise, a fresh patient
tumor expanded biomass in the first three days after MOS generation,
comparable with patient-derived tumoroids and fresh PDX samples that
increased biomass. These proof-of-concept experiments in one fresh patient
tumor and one fresh PDX drug screen provide initial evidence that MOS can
support ex vivo testing of fresh material within a short time frame. This is
important, as the long turnaround times that often exceed the median time to
progression [4], have limited the clinical use of patient-derived tumoroids
[9,10,12]. Ex vivo drug screening of fresh tumor tissue shortens turnaround times
[11,22], and the reduced cell input required by MOS could further improve

Chapter 4150
feasibility of screening low-input samples. We could not compare drug response
in MOS with patient response, as this data was not available for these samples.
However, previous studies have shown that MOS responses correlated with
clinical outcome [24,25], and that drug sensitivities could be obtained within ~10
days of sample receipt in adult cancers. Although future studies should expand
this work, as larger pediatric cohorts will be essential to validate clinical
applicability and to correlate drug response with patient outcomes, these findings
suggest that MOS is suited for drug screening within a clinically relevant time
frame, especially for low-input material.
Next to MOS, many complementary 3D ex vivo modelling approaches are
being developed to improve the physiological relevance of in vitro drug testing
[38]. Whole-tissue platforms such as ALTEN preserve intact tumor tissue
architecture and multicellular niches by encapsulating primary tissue fragments
in alginate hydrogels [39]. These approaches are well suited for studying the
native tissue niche and interactions with the TME but are generally less scalable
and allow testing of fewer compounds. In contrast to whole-tissue platforms,
patient-derived tumoroids provide high scalability and long-term expansion,
making them suitable for compound discovery and biomarker research. However,
patient-derived tumoroids require longer establishment times. MOS, in
contrast, is optimized for the rapid generation and short-term expansion of tumor
cells from freshly dissociated low-input samples, enabling reproducible and
scalable drug sensitivity testing within clinically relevant timelines which is
especially useful for guiding clinical decision-making. Successful MOS
generation depends on the quality and viability of the starting material after
mechanical and enzymatic dissociation, which may vary between samples. In
addition, MOS cultures rely on Matrigel, which introduces an extracellular
matrix environment that must be tolerated by tumor cells. In our study, using
MOS allowed parallel testing up to 90 compounds while maintaining 3D growth
conditions. As such, MOS is particularly suited for precision medicine
applications, where speed is crucial.
This study did not investigate tumor TME retention, although previous work
has shown that MOS can preserve stromal components [24]. Exploring if
neuroblastoma MOS retain elements of the TME will be an important next step

MicroOrganoSphereTM technology to advance drug
screening in neuroblastoma precision medicine1514
for assessing compound activity in a more patient representative setting. In
patient samples where other cell types are present, tumor-specific markers, such
as NCAM, B7H3 and L1CAM, could be used to distinguish tumor from non-tumor
responses. In addition, MOS have been shown to support efficient CAR-T cell
infiltration and killing, indicating their potential for immunotherapy testing [26].
In addition, culture conditions such as hypoxia have been proposed to better
recapitulate aspects of the neuroblastoma tumor niche [40,41]. While hypoxia
was not investigated in the present study, MOS cultures can be maintained
under controlled oxygen conditions after generation. Finally, it should be noted
that ex vivo drug screening does not capture in vivo pharmacokinetic and
pharmacodynamic processes. Factors such as plasma protein binding, drug
lipophilicity and tissue distribution can influence effective drug exposure at the
tumor site and should be considered when translating ex vivo drug sensitivity
results to clinical applications [42–44]. Future studies of neuroblastoma MOS
screening could include evaluation of TME preservation, testing of
immunotherapies, hypoxia culture, and better representing pharmacokinetic and
pharmacodynamic processes.
Conclusion
This proof-of-concept demonstrates that MOS technology supports the ex vivo
growth and drug screening of neuroblastoma cells, including low-input samples,
within clinically relevant time frames. Future studies should focus on expanding
pediatric patient cohorts, assessing clinical applicability and comparing drug
response to clinical outcome, to validate MOS as a functional precision
medicine platform for preclinical drug testing.

Chapter 5162
Abstract
High-risk neuroblastoma patients face poor survival despite intensive treatment.
Drug testing using patient-derived models can support therapy prioritization for
precision medicine and drug development. Models incorporating tumour
microenvironmental components, such as co-cultures and short-term cultured
patient samples containing substantial non-malignant cell fractions, could better
recapitulate microenvironment-dependent drug responses. However,
conventional viability assays measure the combined signal from all viable cells in
a well and therefore cannot determine tumour-specific drug responses. Here, we
establish a microscopy-based readout to quantify cell-type-specific viability in
two complementary settings: neuroblastoma-PBMC co-cultures and freshly
dissociated patient tumour samples. In the co-cultures, PBMCs were pre-labelled
with a cell-tracking dye, and Calcein staining was used to independently quantify
the viability of tumour cells and PBMCs in the same well. The Calcein-based
viability readout correlated strongly with conventional CellTiter-Glo
measurements and was compatible with automated high-throughput drug
screening. The imaging workflow enabled identification of compounds with
differential efficacy in co-culture versus monoculture and distinguished tumour-
specific effects from PBMC toxicity. The microscopy-based viability readout was
further adapted to short-term cultured patient samples. Neuroblastoma tumour
cells were distinguished from the non-malignant cells using a combination of
tumour-specific surface markers NCAM, L1CAM and B7H3. This enabled
determination of tumour fractions and measurement of tumour-specific drug
responses. Tumour fractions varied substantially between patient samples,
highlighting the importance of tumour-specific viability measurements.
Together, the microscopy-based viability readout for co-cultures and patient
samples enables scalable assessment of tumour-specific drug responses.
