Introduction
Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest progenitor cells of the developing
sympathetic nervous system and is the most common extra-cranial solid tumour
in children. 1,2 Despite intensive multimodal treatment, high-risk neuroblastoma
remains associated with poor outcome, with 5-year overall survival rates of
approximately 50%.2,3 In addition, survivors often experience severe long-term
treatment-related toxicity.4,5 This highlights the need for more effective and
better tailored treatment strategies.
Patient-derived organoids are widely used for drug testing in neuroblastoma. 6–
8 Organoid establishment usually takes several months, but once established,
they are scalable for high-throughput assays which makes them well suited for
drug development. 7–9 Conventional organoid monocultures, however, lack
components of the tumour microenvironment, which can influence drug
response and are essential for evaluating immune-mediated therapies. 10–12 Co-
culture models incorporating immune cells increase physiological relevance
while retaining scalability. However, these assays require readouts that
distinguish tumour viability from immune-cell viability in the same well. 13–16
Furthermore, drug testing on ex vivo short-term cultured patient material,
containing unknown tumour fractions, is increasingly being explored as a
complementary approach to molecular profiling for precision oncology. 8,17–20
Most high-throughput viability assays, including CellTiter-Glo, measure the
combined metabolic activity from all cells present in the well and therefore cannot
distinguish tumour from non-malignant cells.8,21,22 Genetic labelling strategies,
such as luciferase expression, can enable cell-type-specific readouts but require
prior modification of the tumour cells which is time- and labour-intensive and not
feasible for primary patient samples.16 Therefore, scalable, non-genetic, cell-type-
specific viability assays are needed to assess drug responses in physiologically
relevant in vitro models. Immunofluorescent microscopy-based approaches are
increasingly compatible with high-throughput workflows and provide a solution for
tumour-specific viability measurements in co-cultures and patient-derived
samples.21,23–25 Tumour-specific markers, already established in diagnostics and
therapeutic targeting, enable tumour-specific labelling in mixed cell populations.
However, expression of these individual markers is heterogeneous across

Chapter 5164
neuroblastoma samples, which limits the reliability of single-marker
approaches.26–29
By combining viability dyes with either pre-labelling of PBMCs or a cocktail of
tumour-specific surface markers, we establish a microscopy-based viability
readout that enables separate quantification of tumour and non-tumour viability
in neuroblastoma-PBMC co-cultures and patient samples.
Methods
Detailed experimental procedures, including model establishment, culture
conditions, CellTracker Orange (CTO) retention after T-cell activation, drug
screening methods, imaging settings and data processing pipelines, are provided
in the Supplementary Methods.
Shared methodology
In short, two organoid lines from distinct tumour sites of the same patient6 were
used throughout the study: AMC691T, (primary tumour; mesenchymal phenotype;
HLA+) and AMC691B (bone marrow metastasis; adrenergic phenotype; HLA -).
A compound library of 134 compounds was screened in 6 concentrations in a
384-well format. Viability was normalized to vehicle-treated controls and the area
under the curve (AUC) was determined from the dose-response curves. Quality
control included assessment of growth rates, positive and negative controls,
replicate consistency, and visual inspection of curve fits of individual curves and
the overall screen.
Neuroblastoma-immune co-cultures
In short, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were obtained from
healthy donors (Mini Donor Bank; institutional review board approval at UMCU:
TC18-774), isolated using Ficoll density gradient centrifugation 30 and
cryopreserved at -180 °C until use.
Organoids were seeded in 384-well plates and co-cultured with PBMCs, which
were pre-labelled with CTO to enable distinction between tumour and immune
cells during image analysis. Co-cultures were established at an effector-to-target
ratio of 1:5 and exposed to compounds for 120 hours.

A microscopy-based readout to assess tumour-specific viability in
neuroblastoma co-cultures and short-term cultured patient samples1655
At readout, viable cells were stained using Calcein Violet (CalceinV) and imaged
using the high-content confocal microscope Opera Phenix (5x air objective;
confocal mode). One fixed Z-plane was selected based on comparison with a five-
plane z-stack and its maximal intensity projection. CellTiter-Glo 3D (CTG) assays
were performed after imaging for multiple plates, to benchmark the microscopy-
based viability readout against conventional whole-well viability
measurements. 7,8,22
Image analysis was performed in Harmony software (Revvity). PBMCs were
identified as CTO+ regions. All viable cells were defined as CalceinV⁺ regions.
Viable PBMCs were then defined as overlapping CTO+/CalceinV + regions and
viable tumour cells as CalceinV+ regions subtracting the viable PBMC mask. The
viability (CalceinV) was quantified using the sum pixel intensity of images.
Compounds showing intrinsic autofluorescence that interfered with signal
detection (Suppl. Table 1) were excluded from downstream analyses in the
affected channel.
Patient-derived samples
In short, patient-derived tumour samples were obtained through institutionally
approved biobank protocols of the Erasmus Medical Center Rotterdam (MEC-
2016-793) and the Princess Máxima Center (PMCLAB2022.370). Freshly
dissociated samples were short-term cultured prior to plating in round-bottom
384-well plates. To distinguish tumour from non-malignant cells, a
neuroblastoma-specific antibody cocktail (NB-cocktail) targeting NCAM, L1CAM
and B7H3 conjugated to a far-red fluorophore was combined with the viability
dye CalceinAM. Neuroblastoma samples (MaxPatient1-3) were cultured for 4–7
days prior to screening, whereas one melanotic neuroectodermal tumour of
infancy sample (MaxPatient4) was cultured for one month until screening was
performed.
Images were acquired using optimized confocal microscopy settings (10x
objective; single-field acquisition; 6 z-planes) and analysed using mask-based
segmentation workflows. Viable tumour cells were defined as NB-
cocktail+/CalceinAM+ and total viable cells as CalceinAM+. The sum of the
integrated pixel intensities of the CalceinAM signal was determined in both
populations. Tumour fractions were calculated as the ratio of viable tumour cells to

Chapter 5166
total viable cells. For proof-of-principle drug testing, patient-derived samples were
exposed to selected compounds and tumour-specific viability was quantified within
tumour-marker+ populations.
Results
Optimization of a microscopy-based viability readout
To enable microscopy-based measurement of viability in neuroblastoma-immune
co-cultures, we first optimized and validated technical aspects of the readout
method. We utilized two organoid lines derived from distinct tumour regions of
the same patient: AMC691T and AMC691B (Fig. 1A).6 AMC691T represents the
mesenchymal phenotype and expresses MHC-I (HLA +), enabling interaction with
immune cells, such as cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells. In contrast,
AMC691B represents the more typical adrenergic neuroblastoma phenotype and
lacks MHC-I expression (HLA-), thereby limiting immune recognition. This
allowed us to model phenotypic heterogeneity regarding tumour-immune
interactions while keeping other properties of the models as similar as possible.
To validate CalceinV as a reliable measure of cell viability, we benchmarked this
imaging-based readout against the luminescence-based assay CTG, the current
standard for drug screens in monocultures of organoids. 8 Calcein Violet
(CalceinV) reports on esterase activity in viable cells, whereas CTG quantifies
cellular ATP content (Suppl. Fig. 1A). Microscopy-based CalceinV staining clearly
distinguished viable (vehicle treated) from non-viable (staurosporine treated)
cells (Suppl. Fig. 1B). The coefficients of variation in untreated wells were
comparable between CalceinV and CTG signals, indicating similar assay
reproducibility for both readouts (Fig. 1B; Suppl. Fig. 1C).
To compare drug sensitivities in tumour monocultures, both organoid lines
were screened using a comprehensive drug library (n = 134 compounds).
Comparing area under the dose response curve values (AUC), CalceinV-derived
drug sensitivity correlated strongly with that of CTG (r = 0.88-0.96; Fig. 1C).
Despite their phenotypic differences, overall drug sensitivity was largely
conserved between AMC691T and AMC691B, with differential responses limited
to a small subset of compounds (Suppl. Fig. 1D). Eight compounds, including
prexasertib, showed higher efficacy (ΔAUC ≥ 100) in AMC691B (Suppl. Fig. 1E).

A microscopy-based readout to assess tumour-specific viability in
neuroblastoma co-cultures and short-term cultured patient samples1675
In contrast, five compounds, including cobimetinib, were more effective in
AMC691T (Suppl. Fig. 1E). Together, these results demonstrate that the
microscopy-based readout provides a quantitative and robust measure of cell
viability and drug response.
Distinguishing cell type-specific viability in tumour-immune co-
cultures
To assess cell-type-specific viability in co-culture conditions, peripheral blood
mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from healthy donors were pre-stained with the
proliferation dye CellTracker Orange (CTO) and distinguished from tumour cells
using an image-based masking strategy (Fig. 1D). Downstream analysis pipelines
for co-cultures segmented viable organoids as CalceinV +/CTO - regions and viable
PBMCs as CalceinV +/CTO+ regions. Cell-type specific CalceinV sum intensities
were extracted from both regions. We used this approach to distinguish between
viable and non-viable fractions for both cell types present in the co-culture well.
We first assessed the baseline killing of the AMC691T and AMC691B by PBMCs.
Immune mediated differences were expected, since, in contrast to AMC691T,
AMC691B is HLA-, limiting T-cell recognition. Indeed, AMC691T showed reduced
viability in a PBMC co-culture compared to monoculture (Suppl. Fig. 2A),
consistent with PBMC-mediated killing. To achieve ~20% baseline killing, we
tested multiple effector-to-target ratios and found 1:5 consistently optimal across
three donors (Suppl. Fig. 2B). In contrast, the growth of AMC691B was
comparable with and without PBMCs (Suppl. Fig. 2C).
We assessed the stability of CTO labelling over the 120-hour assay duration,
including conditions of immune activation that may induce proliferation and
subsequent dye dilution. PBMC monocultures were stimulated via CD3 signalling to
induce TCR-mediated activation. Under these conditions, CTO loss was minimal:
below 3% of viable cells misclassified as CTO- (Fig. 1E). PBMCs were selected for pre-
labelling rather than organoids because organoids are cultured for an additional 48
hours and generally display higher proliferative capacity, potentially resulting in
greater dye dilution. These results demonstrate that CTO pre-staining enables stable
and reliable identification of immune cells throughout the screening assay.
Finally, to enable high-throughput screening, we automated the readout and
optimized imaging speed by selecting a single Z plane, as described in the methods

Chapter 5168
section. This reduced imaging time approximately two-fold, resulting in ~8
minutes acquisition time per 384-well plate, without compromising signal intensity
(Suppl. Fig. 2D-E). Collectively, these validation experiments established a robust,
scalable cell-type specific microscopy-based readout suitable for high-throughput
drug screening in neuroblastoma-immune co-cultures.

Identifying compound sensitivities in co-cultures using the
microscopy-based readout
Having established and technically validated this microscopy-based readout for
cell-type-specific drug responses, we next applied it to high-throughput drug
testing in organoid-PBMC co-cultures (Fig. 2A). In short, organoids were seeded
in 384-well plates. Two days later (t = 0 h), pre-labelled PBMCs were added to
the organoids and compounds were added for 120 hours. At readout, the viability
dye CalceinV was added and automated image acquisition was performed. The
drug library was screened across both conditions in the two organoid lines,
AMC691T and AMC691B.
To identify compounds with altered efficacy in the presence of PBMCs, we
compared drug responses between mono- and co-culture conditions (Fig. 2B). A
clear distinction was observed between the two organoid models, in accordance
with their immune status. Specifically, there were several compounds with
altered efficacy in co- versus monoculture for AMC691T, whereas in AMC691B
almost no differences were observed (Fig. 2B). In AMC691T, five compounds
showed increased efficacy in the co-culture (ΔAUC ≥ 50), and 22 compounds
showed reduced efficacy, in contrast to AMC691B where only 3 and 2 compounds
showed increased and reduced efficacy, respectively. No overlapping compounds
with altered efficacy were identified between the two organoid lines. In AMC691T,
AZD5582 demonstrated greater efficacy in co-culture compared to monoculture
(ΔAUC = 197; Fig. 2C-D; Suppl. Fig. 3), suggesting a PBMC-mediated effect. In
line with this, AZD5582 did not exert toxic effects on PBMCs at concentrations
below 10 μM (Fig. 2C). Similarly, vinblastine showed increased efficacy in co-
culture (ΔAUC = 50), with PBMCs remaining viable at high concentrations (Fig.
2C-D; Suppl. Fig. 3). Together, these results demonstrate the applicability of this
microscopy-based approach to identify compounds with altered efficacy in co-
culture conditions, potentially informing the selection of compounds for
combination with immunotherapy.
To identify compounds with tumour-selective efficacy, we directly compared
tumour cell and PBMC responses from the same wells, as limiting PBMC toxicity
may preserve immune-mediated anti-tumour activity in vivo. We identified 6
compounds that were consistently more effective in tumour cells in both organoid
lines (ΔAUC ≥ 100 in organoids vs PBMCs in both lines), comprising 5

Chapter 5172
microtubule-targeting agents (docetaxel, paclitaxel, vindesine, vinblastine and
vincristine) and antimetabolite gemcitabine (Fig. 2E). For example, docetaxel
and paclitaxel induced tumour killing at low concentrations (0.001 μM and 0.01
μM, respectively), while PBMC viability was unaffected up to 10 μM (Fig. 2F-G).
Additional tumour-selective compounds were identified in only one of the two
organoid lines, with two compounds specific for AMC691T and 30 for AMC691B
(Suppl. Fig. 4A). The AMC691B-specific compounds included prexasertib,
decitabine, alisertib and carboplatin, which were already more effective in
AMC691B monocultures and did not affect PBMC viability. Together, these
results demonstrate that the microscopy-based readout enables identification of
tumour-selective compounds that may be relevant for combination strategies
with immunotherapies.
We next assessed compounds with comparable effects on tumour and immune
cells, as the toxicity of the compounds on the immune cells may be a reason to
not apply them in vivo. Compounds were selected based on efficacy in both cell
types (AUC < 400) and limited differences in viability reduction between PBMCs
and organoids (|ΔAUC| < 100). We identified six compounds, the proteasome
inhibitors bortezomib and ixazomib, the HDAC inhibitors romidepsin and
fimepinostat, β-catenin antagonist tegavivint and CDK12/13 inhibitor SR-4835,
with similar activity in tumour cells and PBMCs across both organoid lines
(Suppl. Fig. 4B-C). No compounds were consistently more toxic to PBMCs versus
organoids across the full dose-response range (ΔAUC ≥ 100 in PBMCs versus
organoid in both lines). Overall, this data demonstrates the applicability of this
readout for high-throughput drug screening in tumour-immune co-cultures,
enabling assessment of compounds with enhanced or decreased efficacy in co-
cultures, tumour-specific effects, and potential PBMC toxicity.

Development and validation of a microscopy-based readout to
determine tumour-specific viability in patient-derived samples
In short-term cultured patient material, which still contains the tumour
microenvironment, it is essential to assess tumour-specific viability, similar to the
co-cultures described above. To distinguish tumour from their
microenvironmental cells, we developed a microscopy-based readout for use in
primary patient material.
To enable drug testing in low-input patient samples, we optimized the assay for
reduced cell numbers per well. Standard flat-bottom assays typically require
~5000 cells per well, which is not feasible for testing multiple compounds on
minimally invasive biopsies. 8,22 Therefore, we adapted the assay to round-bottom
384-well plates to improve cell viability and promote spheroid growth from a
limited cell density (500 cells/well). Round-bottom plates pose challenges for
automated microscopy due to potential focus errors, as consecutive autofocus
failures lead to termination of automated image acquisition. To address this, we
optimized imaging settings using the two organoid models by systematically
comparing objective magnification and numbers of field-of-view and selecting for
the lowest amount of focus errors. Imaging with a 10× objective and a single
central field resulted in zero focus errors, whereas imaging with multiple fields or
the 5x magnification increased error rates substantially (n = 28 and 5,
respectively; Suppl. Fig. 5A). Additionally, using only one field of view imaged 42
wells in 4 minutes versus 13 minutes for the 4 fields of view condition. Therefore,
we selected the 10x objective with one central field of view, imaging the centre of
the well while excluding the well edges. These optimized imaging settings enabled
robust and fast image acquisition in round-bottom plates with a reduced cell
input of 500 cells per well.
Patient material is more complex than neuroblastoma-PBMC co-culture
systems, because tumour cells must be distinguished from multiple non-
malignant cell types. As these cells cannot be selectively pre-labelled prior to
plating, tumour cells were identified using a far-red-conjugated neuroblastoma-
specific antibody cocktail targeting NCAM, L1CAM and B7H3 (NB-cocktail).
These markers are widely used in neuroblastoma diagnostics and are being
explored as therapeutic targets due to their high expression on tumour cells and
limited expression in surrounding stromal and immune cells.26–29 By combining

A microscopy-based readout to assess tumour-specific viability in
neuroblastoma co-cultures and short-term cultured patient samples1775
these markers with the viability dye CalceinAM Green (CalceinAM), it is possible
to identify viable neuroblastoma cells as NB-cocktail +/CalceinAM + and non-
neuroblastoma viable cells as NB-cocktail -/CalceinAM + (Fig. 3A).
We first evaluated the tumour markers both individually and combined on two
organoid models by quantifying CalceinAM intensity within each marker-defined
population. The adrenergic organoid line AMC691B showed strong positivity for
all three markers, whereas its mesenchymal counterpart AMC691T was positive
for B7H3 but showed minimal expression of NCAM and L1CAM (Fig. 3B-C;
Suppl. Fig. 5B). Combining all three markers into a single neuroblastoma-specific
antibody cocktail resulted in robust detection of tumour cells in both organoids
while PBMC controls showed minimal signal (Fig. 3B). We then tested the
sensitivity and specificity of the NB-cocktail setup in a co-culture of AMC691B
organoids with pre-labelled PBMCs and observed that the NB-cocktail
distinguished tumour from immune cells (Suppl. Fig. 5C-E), with minimal
overlap between the NB-cocktail and PBMC-specific eFluor450 signals. The
combination of three tumour markers is particularly advantageous for patient-
derived samples, where (individual) marker expression is not determined prior
to the assay.
Tumour-specific viability and drug responses in short-term cultured
patient samples
To apply the established microscopy-based readout to ex vivo tumour material,
we obtained three neuroblastoma patient samples (two biopsies and one
resection) and one melanocytic neuroectodermal tumour of infancy sample
(MNTI; resection; Suppl. Table 2). This rare paediatric tumour was included to
demonstrate broader applicability of the workflow, since it was confirmed B7H3
positive by pathology.
We analysed the viability of the tumour and non-tumour fractions at baseline and
during short-term culture. The MNTI sample (MaxPatient4) consisted almost
entirely of tumour cells at t = 0 h (99%), whereas tumour fractions varied
substantially across the neuroblastoma samples, ranging from 22% (MaxPatient3) to
66% (MaxPatient2), with MaxPatient1 at 55% (Fig. 3D-E; Suppl. Fig. 6A-B). These
findings underscore the importance of tumour-specific viability measurements, as
drug responses of tumour cells may be masked by large non-malignant cell fractions.

Chapter 5178
Marker expression also varied between patients. MaxPatient2 showed higher
expression of B7H3 and NCAM compared to L1CAM, whereas MaxPatient3 was
positive for L1CAM and NCAM, but showed lower B7H3 expression (Suppl. Fig. 6C).
Together, these results support the use of the NB-cocktail in patient samples with
different marker expression profiles and demonstrate the applicability of the readout
to determine tumour fractions and tumour-specific viability.
We next assessed whether this readout can be applied to determine tumour-
specific drug responses in short-term cultured patient samples. Because of the
limited amount of tumour material, we selected a small number of compounds to
test at a single concentration as a proof-of-concept. Staurosporine was included as
a cytotoxic compound. Vincristine was selected based on the use in standard
neuroblastoma treatment regimens and, together with cytarabine, showed limited
PBMC toxicity in our co-culture experiments. Due to the limited availability of
viable tumour cells in MaxPatient1, only a single compound was tested. Viability
was quantified within tumour-specific masks and compared with total cell viability
(Suppl. Fig. 7A). The low tumour fraction at t = 0 h for MaxPatient3 (Fig. 3D; Suppl.
Fig. 6A) was reflected by a clear difference between total and tumour-specific
viability at the drug screen readout (t = 72 h; Suppl. Fig. 7A). In contrast, the MNTI
sample MaxPatient4 showed more similar total and tumour-specific viability,
consistent with the high tumour fraction. In addition, the neuroblastoma samples
showed limited changes in viability during the assay (75-115% viability from 0 h to
72 h), whereas the MNTI sample did proliferate (146%).
Cytotoxicity could clearly be detected using this microscopy-based readout, as
staurosporine (10 μM) induced cell death compared to the vehicle control (0.25%
DMSO; Fig. 3F-G; Suppl. Fig. 7A-B). Tubulin inhibitor vincristine (1 μM) and
DNA polymerase inhibitor cytarabine (10 μM) showed limited efficacy in the
neuroblastoma samples, likely reflecting the limited cell proliferation (Suppl. Fig.
7A). In contrast, vincristine induced cell killing in the MNTI sample, while
cytarabine showed minimal activity. Finally, the MNTI sample provided
sufficient material for a larger drug screen of 44 compounds across the full dose-
response range (Fig. 3H; Suppl. Fig. 7C). Mitoxantrone and daunorubicin were
the most effective compounds. The high tumour fraction allowed for direct
comparison of CTG versus CalceinAM based drug response quantified within the
tumour population, which was highly concordant (r = 0.88; Suppl. Fig. 7D).

Together, this data supports the feasibility and specificity of this microscopy-
based readout for the use of short-term cultured patient samples to determine the
tumour fraction over time and, if sufficient material is available, to test tumour-
specific drug response.

Chapter 5182
Discussion
To advance drug testing in neuroblastoma, a difficult-to-treat paediatric cancer,
we developed a microscopy-based viability readout that enables assessment of
drug responses in the presence of the tumour microenvironment (TME), in both
neuroblastoma-immune co-cultures and short-term cultured patient samples.
This is increasingly relevant as the TME influences drug response and because
immunomodulatory therapies are emerging for neuroblastoma. 10–12 The readout
strongly correlated with conventional viability measurements while providing
additional value through cell type-specific viability quantification. 7,8
The microscopy-readout for organoid-PBMC co-cultures enables direct
comparison of drug effects on tumour cells and PBMCs within the same well, in
contrast to approaches that assess PBMC toxicity in separate monoculture assays
independently from tumour cell viability. 8,31,32 Compounds effective against
tumour cells either showed comparable PBMC toxicity or largely spared PBMC
viability. The latter may preserve anti-tumour immune activity in vivo and
thereby support combination strategies with immunotherapies. Microtubule-
targeting agents were especially effective against tumour cells and had little effect
on PBMC viability. These agents disrupt microtubule dynamics, leading to
mitotic arrest and apoptosis, processes to which highly proliferative cells are
particularly vulnerable.33,34 Both organoid lines proliferated substantially more
than PBMCs in vitro, which may partly explain their dependency on microtubule
dynamics and the resulting cytotoxic selectivity. Although PBMC viability
represents only a limited measure of non-tumour toxicity, this high-throughput
workflow supports identification of tumour-selective compounds to be further
validated in future studies.
Several compounds showed increased efficacy in co-culture compared to
monoculture, including the apoptosis protein antagonist AZD5582 and
microtubule targeting agent vinblastine. Previous studies have indicated
immunomodulatory effects for AZD5582, including enhanced tumour infiltration
by CD8+ T-cells, reduced regulatory T-cell abundance, dendritic cell activation
and improved T-cell priming.35–37 Similarly, vinblastine has been shown to
stimulate anti-tumour immune responses through activation of dendritic cells,

A microscopy-based readout to assess tumour-specific viability in
neuroblastoma co-cultures and short-term cultured patient samples1835
although dendritic cells are present at low frequencies in PBMCs. 38 These
findings illustrate the value of the co-culture screen in scalable detection of
compounds whose efficacy is enhanced by the presence of immune cells.
Prioritized candidates can subsequently be characterized using immune profiling
approaches, including evaluation of their effects on different immune cell
subsets, cytokine production and activation and exhaustion markers. 39
The co-culture readout used allogeneic PBMCs from healthy adult donors to
allow standardization, reproducibility and scalability, but these may not fully
recapitulate the immune composition and dysfunction observed in
neuroblastoma patients. 12,40 Future studies could incorporate autologous patient-
derived immune cells, although limited material from minimally invasive
paediatric procedures remains a challenge. PBMCs represent only part of the
TME and incorporating additional cell types such as stromal cells would increase
physiological relevance. The workflow is also suited for studying emerging
immune-mediated therapies, such as CAR-T cells, which are increasingly relevant
in neuroblastoma and could be incorporated into co-culture screens. 12,41 This co-
culture workflow provides a scalable assay for tumour-immune drug screening,
with potential to inform both immunotherapy development and tumour-selective
compound prioritization in neuroblastoma.
We extended the microscopy-based viability readout to short-term cultured
patient material to quantify tumour fraction and tumour-specific drug response
in mixed cell populations. This addresses an important limitation of current ex
vivo drug screening approaches, which rely on whole-well viability
measurements and cannot distinguish tumour from non-malignant cells.20,19
Combining neuroblastoma-associated markers (L1CAM, NCAM and B7H3)
into a cocktail enabled distinction of tumour cells from surrounding cells,
compensating for intra- and interpatient variability in surface marker expression.
Although these markers are widely used neuroblastoma markers, NCAM can also
be expressed by immune cells (particularly NK cells) and B7H3 can be expressed
by myeloid and endothelial cells in the tumour-microenvironment. 26–29,42–44
Using a threshold-based separation limits false tumour-positive signals, as
neuroblastoma cells have higher surface expression than immune cells. This
microscopy-based viability readout for patient samples can be readily adapted to
other tumour types by substituting tumour-specific markers.

Chapter 5184
Limited viable tumour material remains a challenge for ex vivo short-term
patient screens. 8,19,20,22 Therefore, we reduced the cell density per well.
Neuroblastoma patient samples retained non-malignant cells during short-term
culture, showing variable tumour fractions (22-66%), but tumour cells showed
little to no proliferation during the assay, which likely contributed to the limited
compound responses observed. Longer pre-culture durations may increase viable
tumour cell numbers and proliferation rates but simultaneously change TME
representation, as illustrated in the MNTI sample. After one month of culture, the
MNTI sample consisted almost entirely of tumour cells with an increased
proliferation rate, providing more viable tumour material for screening that
enabled testing of a larger compound panel. The balance between preserving
TME components and obtaining sufficient tumour material requires optimization
based on the research question and available material.
Current precision oncology initiatives such as INFORM and ZERO rely on
whole-well viability measurements for ex vivo drug testing. 19,20 For cultures
containing both tumour and non-malignant cells, tumour-specific viability
assessment provides additional value by distinguishing tumour-specific drug
responses from effects on surrounding non-malignant cells. The predictive value
of ex vivo drug screening for treatment response in patients remains to be
established in large paediatric cohorts. Microscopy-based tumour-specific
viability readouts could contribute to this effort by enabling more precise drug
response measurements, thereby ultimately supporting treatment stratification
in neuroblastoma precision medicine.
Conclusion
We developed a scalable microscopy-based readout that enables cell-type-specific
drug response profiling in neuroblastoma-immune co-cultures and short-term
cultured patient samples that could support future immunotherapy development
and precision medicine.

General Discussion

Chapter 6200
Expanding the precision medicine landscape of pediatric
solid tumors with ex vivo drug screening
Despite scientific advances and intensive multimodal treatment, cancer
remains a leading cause of disease-related death in children. 1 Treatment
strategies in pediatric oncology are shifting away from historical “one-size-fits-
all” chemotherapies by increasingly applying precision medicine to guide
treatment. One approach is molecular profiling (the sequencing of the genome
and transcriptome), which has become standard practice in the Princess
Máxima Center. Although this has improved treatment for selected patients,
molecular profiling alone often fails to identify effective therapies in high-risk
pediatric tumors. 2,3 The poor survival rates for high-risk disease emphasize the
urgent need for more effective treatment strategies and have stimulated
growing interest in functional precision medicine which captures biological
responses in preclinical models.
The studies in this thesis therefore investigated functional precision medicine in
the form of drug screening in preclinical models, aiming to better predict patient
drug response. The following questions form the foundation of this thesis: which
model system is most appropriate for clinical treatment stratification versus drug
and biomarker discovery? How can we further improve our drug screening
methodology? And, importantly, what is the position of drug screening in guiding
treatment decisions? This discussion first evaluates the strengths and limitations
of the preclinical model systems investigated throughout this thesis.
Subsequently, the role and challenges of drug screening in rapidly guiding
treatment decisions are discussed. Finally, opportunities for drug and biomarker
discovery aimed at improving treatment for future patients are considered.
Preclinical models to test drug response
Different preclinical model systems have been developed to evaluate therapeutic
vulnerabilities in pediatric solid tumors, including neuroblastoma, the primary
tumor type throughout this thesis. Each model balances physiological relevance,
scalability, cost and turnaround time differently.

General discussion2016
Patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models retain the major genetic and
transcriptomic characteristics of their originating tumors, as demonstrated in
this thesis (Chapter 2-3) and previous studies. 4–6 However, their suitability for
personalized precision medicine is constrained by low engraftment success, low
scalability, high costs and long establishment times.4–9 To reduce animal testing,
encouraged by regulatory agencies, patient-derived non-animal models are
increasingly being explored as alternatives. 10
In this thesis, previously established PDX models of the ITCC-P4 consortium
were used for ex vivo short-term drug screens, organoid generation and in vivo
compound testing (Chapter 2-4). Dissociated PDX samples resemble primary
patient material while offering easier access and sufficient quantity of viable
tumor cells, enabling protocol optimization and testing of larger compound
libraries.11 We established five new PDX-derived neuroblastoma organoids and
used previously established patient-derived neuroblastoma organoids for drug
screening (Chapter 3). Once established, organoids provided a scalable platform
for drug screens, but, in line with literature, we found that their application for
rapid treatment stratification is limited due to relatively low establishment rates
(23%) and prolonged establishment timelines (3-12 months).3,7–9,12–17 These
timelines often exceed the median progression-free survival of relapsed or high-
risk patients (4-7 months).3 Furthermore, patients continue to receive treatment
during organoid establishment, which may drive tumor evolution and reduce the
organoid’s representation of the current disease state. This was illustrated in
Chapter 2, where two longitudinally obtained Ewing sarcoma samples displayed
different drug responses following disease progression.
Ex vivo short-term screens, where freshly dissociated tumor material is briefly
cultured prior to screening, offer a faster approach for preclinical drug testing. In
this thesis, ex vivo short-term drug screens were completed within 14 days after
tissue receipt (Chapter 2 and 3). We demonstrated the feasibility of this approach
in a pan-cancer cohort, achieving an 82% success rate using PDX-derived tumor
material (Chapter 2). Similarly, ZERO and INFORM demonstrated the feasibility
of integrating ex vivo short-term screens in precision medicine programs as the
rapid turnaround time allows integration into multidisciplinary tumor

Chapter 6202
boards. 18,19 Zooming in on neuroblastoma, ex vivo short-term screens achieved
higher success rates (65% versus 23%) and shorter turnaround times compared
to organoids while retaining drug sensitivity patterns (Chapter 3). In addition, ex
vivo drug responses were comparable with in vivo responses in matched PDX
models for seven out of ten clinically available compounds.
The studies presented in this thesis (Chapter 2-5) indicate that, despite model-
specific differences, major drug sensitivity trends were generally preserved across
different readouts and neuroblastoma model systems. Consequently, selecting
the best model for a particular application can be guided by practical
considerations such as scalability, feasibility and turnaround time. Different
model systems may be best suited for rapid treatment stratification for the patient
of today, or for discovering therapies for the patient of tomorrow.
Guiding treatment decisions in precision oncology for
today’s patient
Rapid drug screening within a clinically relevant timeframe
To identify the most effective treatment for the patient of today, preclinical
models to predict drug sensitivity must be rapid, reproducible and feasible for
low-input samples. Turnaround time is particularly important, as treatment
decisions generally need to be made in a timeframe of days rather than months. 17
The findings presented in this thesis indicate that ex vivo short-term drug
screening is currently the most feasible approach for rapid treatment
stratification as results can be obtained within 14 days (Chapter 2). Furthermore,
emerging international precision medicine initiatives incorporating drug
screening have reported clinical feasibility. The ZERO program demonstrated
that 82% of screens could be completed while patients were still under clinical
care and that ex vivo drug responses more accurately reflected in vivo responses
than actionable molecular markers.19 The INFORM program identified drug
vulnerabilities in 80% of cases lacking actionable high-evidence molecular
alterations, with a median preculture time of four days. 18 These studies support
the potential clinical utility of drug screening as a complementary strategy
alongside molecular profiling in pediatric precision oncology.

General discussion2036
Towards clinical implementation: challenges associated with limited
patient material
Several challenges remain before ex vivo short-term drug screening can be
broadly implemented in clinical practice. One of the major barriers is the limited
quantity and quality of viable tumor material obtained from pediatric patient
samples. 18 Small biopsies obtained through minimally invasive procedures and
the reduced viability of tumor tissue in chemotherapy-treated surgical resections
limit the amount of material available for drug screening. Furthermore, current
pathology workflows, optimized for tissue fixation and genomics rather than
viable tissue preservation, might limit the amount of material available for drug
screening even in cases with sufficient tissue. Close collaboration with
pathologists is important to optimize tissue allocation.
This thesis included both freshly dissociated PDX tumor samples, which
provided relatively large quantities of viable tumor cells, and freshly dissociated
patient samples, where material is often limited (Chapter 2-5). We found that
drug sensitivity patterns were largely conserved between matched drug screens
from patient and PDX samples, indicating that PDX-derived material is a
suitable surrogate for primary patient samples (Chapter 3). However, the high
success rates using PDX samples (82% for ex vivo short-term drug screens in
pan-cancer samples; Chapter 2) likely overestimate achievable success rates of
drug screens from patient samples. Besides the larger amounts of viable tumor
compared to clinical biopsies, PDX samples may be biased toward more
aggressive, and thereby better growing, tumor subclones. 20 Indeed,
experiments using patient samples for ex vivo short-term cultures and drug
screens demonstrated that both drug screen success and the number of
compounds tested were strongly limited in cases of low quantity and quality of
viable tumor cells present in the initial sample (Chapter 4-5). In particular,
cryopreserved biopsy samples failed to establish successful short-term cultures
after thawing (data not included in this thesis). This illustrates that fresh
samples of sufficient quality are needed for successful drug screening,
emphasizing the importance of experimental prioritization and careful
allocation of available tumor material to ensure sufficient cell numbers.

Chapter 6204
Extending the short pre-culture period prior to drug screening may improve
recovery from tissue dissociation, increase viable tumor cell numbers and thereby
improve drug screening success. Future studies could therefore optimize the pre-
culture duration and culture conditions to maximize viable tumor material while
still obtaining drug responses within a clinically relevant timeframe. Importantly,
prolonged culture periods may simultaneously change representation of
microenvironmental cells that influence drug response, thereby potentially
decreasing physiological relevance.
Optimizing drug screening methods for limited patient material
To maximize the utility of limited patient material, screening approaches may be
optimized by either reducing the number of cells required per condition or
limiting the number of conditions to test. In this thesis, round-bottom plates
(Chapter 5) and MicroOrganoSpheres (MOS; Chapter 4) reduced the number
of cells required per condition, increasing the number of compounds that can be
screened using the same amount of input material. Previous work in our group
demonstrated that, compared to flat-bottom plates, round-bottom plates
supported sufficient tumor growth at substantially lower cell densities, enabling
drug screening with fewer cells per condition (data not included in this thesis).
Next to this, the use of round-bottom plates supports 3D spheroid formation
which may better represent the architecture of solid tumors. 13 MOS, 3D droplets
generated by microfluidic droplet formation that encapsulate patient-derived
tumor cells in Matrigel, have previously demonstrated rapid drug screening
results that correlate with in-patient response, while requiring low quantities of
tumor tissue.21–24 We demonstrated that MOS technology supports short-term
tumor cell growth at least as well as suspension cultures. Furthermore, drug
screening in MOS could be performed using fewer cells while maintaining
reproducibility and comparable drug responses compared to suspension. Other
miniaturized 3D tumor avatars are increasingly being explored, such as
engineered 3D tumor models and whole-tissue platforms. 25–31
Additionally, the number of conditions could be reduced by creating tumor type-
specific drug libraries consisting of clinically relevant compounds, including

General discussion2056
standard-of-care agents, targeted therapies and drugs previously identified as
active in that tumor type. Ultimately, patient-specific libraries restricted to
clinically accessible treatment options for an individual patient may further
reduce the number of conditions. Although conceptually attractive, generating
patient-specific libraries would require knowing the clinically available treatment
options upfront and is therefore operationally challenging in routine practice. A
more feasible application may be the use of ex vivo short-term drug screening as
a complementary tool within multi-compound clinical trials, to help prioritize
which trial arm is most likely to benefit an individual patient.
In this thesis, we performed drug screening of only single agents to reduce the
number of conditions to test. However, single agents are rarely efficacious due to
genetic intratumor heterogeneity or acquired resistance and therefore
combination therapies better reflect clinical treatment strategies.32 Testing
combinations in vitro remains challenging due to the limited input material and
practical complexities such as dose selection and scheduling. While combination
and synergy screens are increasingly performed in established model systems, 33–
35 comprehensive testing of clinically relevant multi-agent regimens remains
difficult in ex vivo short-term samples as the number of experimental conditions
rapidly increases with each additional compound. Clinical implementation
therefore requires strategic prioritization of experimental conditions that can be
tested from a single patient sample.
Interpreting drug responses in heterogeneous patient samples
Ex vivo short-term cultures can contain substantial proportions of residual
microenvironmental cells, potentially providing a more representative tumor
model than long-term cultures. However, the presence of these non-malignant
cells may also complicate the interpretation of drug screening results, as these
cells influence drug response and may confound interpretation of tumor-specific
drug sensitivity. 36,37 Currently, tumor purity and microenvironmental
contributions are generally not incorporated into the interpretation of ex vivo
short-term drug screens. This is because the conventional viability readout for
high-throughput drug screening, CellTiter-Glo, measures the combined viability
of all cells present in a well. To address this limitation, we developed a

Chapter 6206
microscopy-based readout to determine tumor-specific viability in ex vivo short-
term cultured neuroblastoma samples, which can be readily adapted to other
tumor types (Chapter 5). Neuroblastoma tumor cells were distinguished from the
non-malignant cells using a combination of tumor-specific surface markers
NCAM, L1CAM and B7H3, which enabled determination of tumor fractions and
measurement of tumor-specific drug responses. Because tumor purity is often
unknown prior to screening, microscopy-based tumor-specific viability readouts
may provide a more reliable assessment of tumor-specific drug response.
Interpreting drug screening results to define drug hits
Beyond generating drug response data, clinical implementation requires robust
strategies for data interpretation, hit prioritization and outcome validation.
Currently, there is no universally accepted definition of a clinically meaningful
drug hit in functional precision oncology, limiting cross-site comparison.
Different institutes use different response metrics, including area under the curve
(AUC), half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50), half-maximal lethal
concentration (LC50) and drug sensitivity scores (DSS), and each has its
advantages and limitations. Across this thesis (Chapter 2-5), AUC-based analyses
were most frequently applied, as AUC values can be determined for both
responders and non-responders, whereas IC50 values cannot be determined
when 50% inhibition is not reached. However, IC50 values are valuable for
comparing drug response when different dose ranges are used, e.g. across
institutes/drug libraries (Chapter 2-3). Importantly, harmonization of dose
ranges and response metrics will be essential for reliable cross-institute
comparisons.
To properly interpret drug sensitivity profiles, both we and others applied outlier
approaches to identify patient-specific vulnerabilities relative to reference
cohorts. Depending on the question, comparisons may be performed within a
tumor type to identify subtype-specific hits, across pan-cancer cohorts to identify
patient-specific vulnerabilities (Chapter 2), or relative to non-malignant control
samples to estimate potential therapeutic selectivity and toxicity (Chapter 3 and
5). Large pan-cancer reference cohorts are currently being established in the
Princess Máxima Center, using drug screening data from ex vivo short-term and

General discussion2076
organoid cultures from PDX and patient samples, to further improve
interpretation of patient screens. The relevance and predictive value of non-
malignant reference cohorts remain to be established. If so, pediatric reference
cohorts could be expanded to include samples derived from tissues such as liver
and colon, which are commonly affected by treatment-related toxicities.
Drug screening in the lab is limited by the incomplete representation of in vivo
pharmacokinetics.38–41 In this thesis (Chapter 2), Cmax values, typically derived
from plasma measurements, were used as a first approximation to assess whether
ex vivo determined IC50 values could be clinically achievable. However,
comparisons between Cmax and IC50 do not account for factors such as plasma
protein binding, drug clearance, tissue distribution and penetration and active
metabolite formation, all of which influence free drug exposure at the tumor
site.42,43 Future studies should therefore incorporate pharmacokinetic
parameters more comprehensively, for example by testing concentrations that
are clinically achievable in the tumor, informed by physiologically based
pharmacokinetic modelling.39–41 In addition, in vitro drug screens typically
expose cells to static drug concentrations for fixed periods of time, whereas
patients experience dynamic drug concentrations due to dosing schedules, drug
clearance and treatment duration. 38 Approaches that better mimic clinical drug
exposure, including compound washout experiments or microfluidic systems,
may therefore further improve the translational value of ex vivo drug
screening.38,44
The greatest challenge for functional precision oncology, and at the same time the
most important limitation of this thesis, remains the correlation of ex vivo short-
term drug responses with clinical outcome. Clinical response data should
ultimately guide selection of both response metrics and hit definition. We
demonstrated concordant ex vivo and in vivo drug responses for seven out of ten
compounds (Chapter 2), but clinical correlations could not yet be assessed within
this thesis. Fortunately, ongoing efforts address this in our center. Encouragingly,
other pediatric precision medicine initiatives demonstrated concordance
between ex vivo short-term drug responses and observed in-patient responses for
selected cases. 18,19,45 Furthermore, promising results are increasingly emerging

Chapter 6208
from adult cancer studies, where the utility of functional precision medicine
approaches is also currently being tested in prospective clinical trials. 3,46 Given
the small patient numbers and biological heterogeneity that characterize
pediatric cancers, international collaboration (such as in Chapter 2 and 3) and
harmonization of drug screening workflows will be essential to generate
sufficiently powered outcome correlations.
Integrating functional testing into clinical decision-making for
today’s patient
To guide treatment decisions alongside molecular profiling, ex vivo drug
responses should ideally be generated within a similar timeframe, allowing
parallel discussion at Molecular Tumor Boards. The integration of both datasets
may provide a higher level of clinical confidence in treatment recommendations.
We demonstrated that ex vivo short-term drug screening can both expand
treatment options for patients lacking targetable molecular alterations and refine
compound selection in the presence of targetable alterations (Chapter 2), which
is consistent with previous reports from precision medicine initiatives INFORM
and ZERO. 18,19 Within the Princess Máxima Center, drug screening results are
discussed in the “Innovation4Care” initiative together with international experts
and the patient’s treating physician. As an example, treatment selection for the
melanocytic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy case (Chapter 5) was supported
by ex vivo short-term drug screening results alongside clinical considerations.
Excitingly, ex vivo short-term drug screening, when further validated, may
ultimately help predict both treatment response and non-response. Early
identification of non-responders is particularly important in pediatric oncology
to avoid unnecessary toxicity and long-term side effects in young children.
Effective treatments for the patients of tomorrow
While functional precision medicine aims to identify the most effective treatment
strategy for the patient of today, drug (combination) and biomarker discovery is
important for treating the patients of tomorrow. Pediatric-specific drug discovery
is particularly important, as pediatric cancers differ fundamentally from adult
malignancies in their developmental origin, relatively low mutational burden and
lower frequency of actionable genomic alterations. Consequently, there is a need

General discussion2096
for pediatric-specific drug and biomarker discovery, including the development
of novel treatment modalities such as antibody-drug conjugates and targeted
protein degraders. International initiatives such as ITCC-P4 and ACCELERATE
play an important role in accelerating development and clinical implementation
of pediatric-specific therapies.
Scalable and biologically representative model systems are required for drug
discovery studies. Compared to ex vivo short-term cultured patient samples,
organoid models are better suited for large-scale drug and biomarker discovery
studies due to their scalability and long-term expandability while retaining key
characteristics of the original tumor. The use of organoid models (cultured
without animal-derived extracellular matrixes) may contribute to reducing
animal-based testing during drug development. Although regulatory agencies
increasingly encourage alternatives to animal experiments,10 PDX models will
likely remain important for late-stage preclinical validation due to their
physiological complexity.
Current organoid models lack a tumor microenvironment, although these cells
influence therapeutic response. The growing clinical importance of
immunotherapies emphasizes the need for scalable, reproducible models
containing different cell types, like co-cultures of organoids with immune cells.
Our microscopy-based cell type-specific viability readout for neuroblastoma-
PBMC co-cultures established in Chapter 5 provides ready-to-use protocols for
high-throughput drug screening that future studies can use for immunotherapy
testing. Integrating other tumor microenvironmental components in co-cultures
may further increase physiological relevance.
Concluding remarks
In summary, the studies presented in this thesis investigated how drug screening
can expand the pediatric precision oncology landscape by evaluating therapeutic
vulnerabilities across multiple model systems of neuroblastoma and other
pediatric solid tumors. Across these studies, ex vivo short-term drug screens
appear feasible within clinically relevant timeframes while largely retaining drug
sensitivity patterns observed in organoids that require substantially longer

Chapter 6210
establishment timelines. Together, these findings demonstrate that different
preclinical model systems fulfill complementary roles within functional precision
oncology. While ex vivo short-term drug screening appears particularly suited for
rapid treatment stratification of the patient of today, scalable organoid models,
preferably incorporating other cell types of the tumor microenvironment, provide
opportunities for drug and biomarker discovery for the patients of tomorrow.
Furthermore, low-input culturing strategies, such as MOS, and tumor-specific
viability readouts may further enhance the feasibility, scalability and clinical
applicability of drug screening. Ultimately, the studies presented in this thesis
support the potential integration of ex vivo short-term drug screening alongside
molecular profiling to improve treatment selection and accelerate development
of more effective therapies for children with difficult-to-treat cancers.

De overlevingskansen voor kinderen met kanker zijn de afgelopen decennia

Bij hoog-risico neuroblastoom, een vorm van kinderkanker, overleeft
bijvoorbeeld slechts de helft van de kinderen de ziekte. Daarnaast kunnen
behandelingen ernstige bijwerkingen veroorzaken, die soms ook op latere
leeftijd nog merkbaar zijn. Daarom is het belangrijk om behandelingen te
identificeren die niet alleen de genezingskansen verbeteren, maar ook minder
schadelijk zijn. Dat vraagt om betere manieren om te bepalen welke
behandeling bij welk kind past. Er bestaan al methoden om behandelingen
beter op de tumor van een patiënt af te stemmen, maar deze leveren niet voor
ieder kind een geschikte behandeloptie op. Dit proefschrift richt zich op
extracraniale solide tumoren bij kinderen. Dit zijn vaste tumoren die ontstaan
in organen of andere weefsels buiten de hersenen. In dit proefschrift
onderzoeken we hoe we kunnen testen welke medicijnen effect hebben op de
tumor van een individueel kind, zodat we in de toekomst beter kunnen bepalen
welke behandeling mogelijk geschikt is. In deze samenvatting bespreken we
eerst enkele begrippen en context die nodig zijn om dit proefschrift te begrijpen.
Daarna leggen we uit waarom het nodig is om het testen van medicijnen op
tumorcellen te verbeteren, en wat we daarvoor in elk hoofdstuk onderzoeken.
Neuroblastoom ontstaat in het zich ontwikkelende zenuwstelsel en komt vooral
voor bij jonge kinderen. De tumor ontstaat vaak in de bijnier, maar kan ook op
andere plaatsen in het lichaam voorkomen. De ziekte kan zich heel verschillend
gedragen: bij sommige kinderen kan de tumor uit zichzelf verdwijnen, terwijl de
ziekte bij anderen agressief groeit en uitzaait. Daarom worden kinderen ingedeeld
in risicogroepen, waarop de behandeling wordt aangepast. Kinderen met een laag
risico kunnen soms met weinig of zelfs zonder behandeling herstellen, terwijl
kinderen met hoog-risico neuroblastoom een intensieve behandeling nodig
hebben. Deze behandeling bestaat bijvoorbeeld uit chemotherapie, een operatie,
stamceltherapie, bestraling en immunotherapie. Ondanks deze intensieve
behandeling komt de ziekte bij meer dan de helft van de kinderen terug of

Om de behandeling te verbeteren, wordt steeds vaker gebruikgemaakt van
precisiegeneeskunde: het afstemmen van de behandeling op de eigenschappen
van de tumor van een individuele patiënt. Hiervoor bestaan twee methoden:
moleculair onderzoek en functionele profilering. In dit proefschrift ligt de nadruk
op functionele profilering. We vergelijken de uitkomsten met die van moleculair
onderzoek, dat momenteel standaard wordt ingezet bij kinderkanker, om te
onderzoeken of beide methoden elkaar kunnen aanvullen. Bij moleculair
onderzoek worden het DNA en RNA van de tumor onderzocht op afwijkingen
waarvoor mogelijk al een gericht medicijn bestaat. Deze aanpak heeft de
behandeling voor een deel van de patiënten verbeterd. Toch biedt moleculair
onderzoek niet voor iedere patiënt een oplossing. Soms wordt er geen geschikte
afwijking gevonden, bestaat er nog geen doelgericht medicijn voor, of werkt een
veelbelovend doelgericht medicijn minder goed dan verwacht. Daarom zijn
aanvullende methoden nodig die kunnen helpen om te bepalen welke medicijnen
daadwerkelijk effect hebben op de tumorcellen van een patiënt.
Functionele profilering is een veelbelovende aanvulling waarbij onderzoekers
rechtstreeks medicijntesten uitvoeren op tumorcellen. Hiervoor worden
tumorcellen buiten het lichaam (ex vivo) in het laboratorium gekweekt en
blootgesteld aan medicijnen. Zo kunnen onderzoekers meten of een medicijn de
tumorcellen kan doden of remmen. Dit kan op drie verschillende manieren, met
drie verschillende modellen. De eerste manier is het gebruik van kortdurende ex
vivo kweken. Hierbij worden tumorcellen tijdelijk in het laboratorium gekweekt,
zodat de effecten van medicijnen relatief snel kunnen worden getest. De tweede
manier is het gebruik van organoïden. Organoïden zijn kleine, vaak
driedimensionale, “mini-organen” die in het laboratorium worden gekweekt. In dit
proefschrift gebruiken we organoïden die gemaakt zijn van tumorcellen (“mini-
tumoren”). Het duurt enkele maanden voordat deze organoïden stabiel groeien,
maar daarna kunnen ze langdurig worden gekweekt, waardoor er veel meer cellen

Appendices218
beschikbaar komen. De derde manier is het gebruik van muismodellen. Hierbij
laten onderzoekers tumorweefsel van een patiënt in een muis groeien. Zo kunnen
zij onderzoeken hoe een behandeling werkt in een levend organisme. Deze
modellen bieden verschillende mogelijkheden voor medicijnonderzoek, maar
hebben elk ook beperkingen. Het was bovendien nog niet duidelijk in hoeverre de
uitkomsten van deze drie modellen met elkaar overeenkomen.
Voordat functionele profilering kan worden gebruikt om behandelkeuzes voor
individuele patiënten te ondersteunen, moet de methode aan drie eisen voldoen.
Ten eerste moet de methode haalbaar zijn met de kleine hoeveelheid
patiëntmateriaal die beschikbaar is, uit bijvoorbeeld een klein naaldbiopt.
Daarnaast is snelheid belangrijk: de methode moet snel genoeg resultaten
opleveren om de behandelkeuze te kunnen beïnvloeden. Tot slot moet de
methode een betrouwbare voorspelling geven van hoe de patiënt écht op het
medicijn zal reageren. De huidige methoden voldoen nog niet optimaal aan deze
eisen. Dit proefschrift richt zich daarom op het verbeteren van functionele
profilering voor extracraniale solide tumoren bij kinderen. In de volgende
hoofdstukken onderzoeken we hoe we veel medicijnen snel kunnen testen
(Hoofdstuk 2), hoe de drie modellen zich tot elkaar verhouden (Hoofdstuk 3), hoe
we met minder tumorcellen kunnen testen (Hoofdstuk 4) en hoe we tumorcellen
kunnen onderscheiden van andere cellen in een tumor (Hoofdstuk 5).
In Hoofdstuk 2 staat de methodologie centraal. We onderzoeken of kortdurende
ex vivo kweken kunnen helpen om snel mogelijke behandelopties voor kinderen
met solide tumoren te vinden. Hiervoor gebruikten we tumoren die in
muismodellen waren gegroeid. We onderzochten negen verschillende tumortypen
en testten per tumorsample de werking van ruim tweehonderd medicijnen. De
resultaten waren binnen twee weken beschikbaar en bleken betrouwbaar en
reproduceerbaar: in twee verschillende instituten vonden we dezelfde
medicijngevoeligheden bij samples van dezelfde patiënt. We onderzochten ook of
met moleculair onderzoek gevonden genetische afwijkingen samenhingen met de
gevoeligheid voor bepaalde medicijnen en vonden dat een genetische afwijking niet
altijd leidde tot meer ex vivo gevoeligheid. Daarnaast konden we voor bijna alle
onderzochte samples één of meerdere medicijnen aanwijzen die uitzonderlijk

Appendices219A
effectief waren ten opzichte van de andere samples. Voor de meeste samples zonder
genetische afwijkingen konden we met deze methode mogelijke alternatieve
behandelopties vinden. Ook bij samples met een bekende genetische afwijking
kunnen kortdurende ex vivo kweken helpen om verschillende medicijnen te
vergelijken die op die afwijking aangrijpen. Kortdurende ex vivo kweken zouden
moleculair onderzoek dus kunnen aanvullen.
In Hoofdstuk 3 richten we ons op neuroblastoom en vergelijken we drie
modellen om tumorweefsel te onderzoeken: kortdurende ex vivo kweken,
organoïden en muismodellen. Waar voldoende materiaal beschikbaar was,
maakten we alle drie de modellen van tumorweefsel van dezelfde patiënt. Zo
konden we de modellen vergelijken op medicijngevoeligheid, snelheid en
haalbaarheid. In de vergelijkingen die we konden uitvoeren, kwamen de gemeten
medicijngevoeligheden grotendeels overeen, maar de modellen verschilden in
haalbaarheid en snelheid. Kortdurende ex vivo kweken waren sneller en beter
haalbaar en lieten vergelijkbare medicijngevoeligheden zien als organoïden en
muismodellen. Daarom lijken kortdurende ex vivo kweken veelbelovend om snel
een behandeling voor een individuele patiënt te kiezen. Organoïden waren
lastiger op te kweken, maar waren, wanneer ze eenmaal goed groeien, juist
geschikt voor grootschalig onderzoek naar nieuwe medicijnen. Muismodellen
kunnen waardevol zijn om veelbelovende behandelingen verder te onderzoeken
in een levend organisme, voordat ze bij patiënten worden onderzocht.
In Hoofdstuk 4 staat de haalbaarheid centraal. We onderzoeken hoe we
medicijntesten haalbaarder kunnen maken met de beperkte hoeveelheid
patiëntmateriaal die beschikbaar is, door ze efficiënter uit te voeren. Hiervoor
gebruikten we de MicroOrganoSphere™-technologie, waarbij tumorcellen in
zeer kleine druppels van een gel groeien en driedimensionale clusters vormen.
We lieten zien dat neuroblastoomcellen hierin minstens even goed groeiden als
met de gebruikelijke kweekmethode. Daarnaast konden we betrouwbare
medicijntesten uitvoeren met 2,5 keer minder tumorcellen, terwijl de resultaten
vergelijkbaar bleven. Hierdoor kunnen we met hetzelfde tumorweefsel een
hoger aantal medicijnen testen. Dit kan vooral waardevol zijn wanneer slechts
een klein stukje tumor beschikbaar is.

Appendices220
In Hoofdstuk 5 verbeteren we de techniek voor samples waarin meerdere
celtypen aanwezig zijn. We ontwikkelen een methode waarbij we een microscoop
gebruiken om celtype-specifieke gevoeligheid voor medicijnen te kwantificeren.
Een tumor bestaat niet alleen uit tumorcellen, maar ook uit omliggende cellen,
waaronder immuuncellen. Deze cellen vormen samen de tumor-micro-omgeving
en kunnen invloed hebben op de reactie van de tumor op een behandeling.
Daarnaast richten steeds meer nieuwe behandelingen zich op het activeren van
het eigen immuunsysteem tegen de tumor. Bij de huidige medicijntesten worden
de reacties van verschillende celtypen vaak gezamenlijk gemeten. Daardoor is
niet altijd duidelijk of een medicijn vooral de tumorcellen of juist de omliggende
cellen beïnvloedt. We ontwikkelden daarom een microscopiemethode die de
tumorcellen apart kan herkennen tussen de andere celtypen. We pasten deze
methode toe op kweken van neuroblastoom organoïden met immuuncellen en op
kortdurende ex vivo kweken van vers patiëntmateriaal. Met deze methode
kunnen we beter onderzoeken welke medicijnen rechtstreeks effect hebben op
tumorcellen en of de aanwezigheid van immuuncellen de werking van een
medicijn verandert.
Tot slot worden in Hoofdstuk 6 de bevindingen van dit proefschrift in
perspectief geplaatst. Er bestaat niet één model dat voor alle onderzoeksvragen
het beste is. Voor de patiënt van vandaag, waarbij snel een behandelbeslissing
nodig is, zijn kortdurende ex vivo kweken veelbelovend omdat ze binnen korte
tijd resultaten opleveren. Voor de patiënt van morgen, waarvoor we nieuwe
medicijnen en combinaties kunnen ontwikkelen, zijn organoïden waardevoller
omdat zij op grotere schaal gebruikt kunnen worden. De grootste openstaande
uitdaging is het aantonen dat de uitkomsten van medicijntesten in het lab
daadwerkelijk voorspellen hoe een patiënt op diezelfde behandeling zal reageren.
Wanneer dit lukt, is het testen van medicijnen op tumorcellen in het lab een
waardevolle aanvulling op moleculair onderzoek. Door genetische informatie te
combineren met medicijntesten op tumorcellen in het lab, kan het landschap van
precisiegeneeskunde worden verbreed en kunnen behandelkeuzes in de toekomst
mogelijk beter worden afgestemd op ieder individueel kind met kanker.

Appendices232
Curriculum Vitae
Marlinde Schoonbeek was born on April 28th, 1998, in Haren, the Netherlands. She
obtained her high school degree at Praedinius Gymnasium in Groningen in 2016
and then began a bachelor’s in Biomedical Sciences at Utrecht University. In 2019,
she started the master’s program in Cancer, Stem Cells and Developmental Biology
at Utrecht University, graduating cum laude in 2021. During her master’s, she
conducted research on extracellular vesicles and the cell cycle (Regenerative
Medicine Centre, Utrecht), paediatric leukaemia (Princess Máxima Centre), and
CDK4/6 inhibition in breast cancer (Dana-Farber Cancer Institute).
She began her career in 2021 as an education developer for the bachelor’s
program in Biomedical Sciences, focusing on data science, career orientation,
student well-being and professional skills. In May 2022, Marlinde started her
PhD research in the Molenaar group at the Princess Máxima Centre. Her research
focused on improving preclinical models for determining drug sensitivity in
neuroblastoma and other paediatric solid tumours. She collaborated with the
biotechnology company Xilis B.V. and a large public-private consortium with
academic institutions, contract research organizations and pharmaceutical
companies. She received the Scholar-in-Training Award at the AACR Precision
Medicine conference in Boston and the Young Investigator Award at Innovation
for Health in Leiden and delivered plenary presentations at both events. She also
received a personal travel grant from Villa Joep.
Alongside her scientific work, Marlinde has organized activities on personal
development, leadership and inclusion. She is a Junior Ambassador for TOPX, a
network for ambitious women in life sciences, where she enjoys organizing and
moderating events and panel discussions. At the Princess Máxima Center,
Marlinde was part of Ace, a community promoting authenticity for excellence in
science through role model lunches, coaching programs and workshops.
Since October 2026, Marlinde works as Application Specialist at the biotechnology
start-up Orgonex. Here, she helps drive the growth and development of the company
and supports researchers and companies in making organoid culture more efficient.
